questions.q: Why does the lecturer open MGMT 2130 with three questions?
options: To test students' prior knowledge of ethics frameworks
To surface students' existing assumptions and motivations
To establish classroom rules and expectations
To preview the final exam format
To divide the class into study groups
questions.explain: The three opening questions explicitly surface students' personal motivations, prior interests, and baseline knowledge. The course does not apply a single mechanical ethical framework but develops awareness and mindset — answering these questions at the outset calibrates students' readiness.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the core premise underlying MGMT 2130?
options: Every person is responsible only for their own decisions
No one is an island; professional decisions unavoidably affect others
Business ethics should only apply to senior management
Ethics are context-specific and cannot be generalized
Shareholder profit is the sole measure of ethical business
questions.explain: The course premise is that no one is an island (孤島) — every professional decision unavoidably affects others. Unclear thinking leads to suboptimal decisions and serious consequences, which is why the course develops awareness rather than rigid frameworks.

questions.q: What method did P&G's analysis department use to obtain Unilever's confidential documents?
options: Corporate espionage via computer hacking
Dumpster diving (翻垃圾桶) by a contractor
Bribing a Unilever employee
Reverse-engineering product samples
Filing a public records request
questions.explain: The P&G case explicitly states the method was 'dumpster diving' by a contractor. This method was legal but ethically contested, illustrating that legality (合法性) and ethics (倫理) are not the same.

questions.q: In the P&G Unilever case, how did P&G's Chairman respond after discovering the competitive intelligence breach?
options: He denied all knowledge and blamed the contractor
He immediately halted the campaign, fired three managers, confessed to Unilever, and reached a settlement
He quietly destroyed the documents and continued with P&G's plans
He negotiated a business deal with Unilever in exchange for silence
He appealed the legality of dumpster diving in court
questions.explain: John E. Pepper's response was immediate and transparent: halt the campaign, fire responsible managers, confess directly to Unilever, and reach a multi-million dollar settlement. This demonstrates accountability beyond legal minimum.

questions.q: What is the primary ethical issue in the P&G dumpster diving case?
options: P&G failed to purchase the information through proper channels
The action was legal but still raised ethical concerns about harm and fairness
P&G's method was more expensive than traditional market research
Unilever immediately discovered the breach and sued
The documents were of little competitive value
questions.explain: The exam trap is that dumpster diving was NOT illegal — the ethical issue arose precisely because the action was legal yet still harmful. This separates legality from ethics, a core course theme.

questions.q: In the Hong Kong speeding bus case, what concept does the discussion connect to?
options: Driver negligence and insurance liability
The ability to respond — a precondition for responsibility (責任能力)
Passenger safety regulations and enforcement
Government traffic control systems
Bus company profit margins and maintenance
questions.explain: The case explores responsibility (責任) and connects to 'ability to respond' — a precondition for responsibility. It raises questions about how drivers should respond to passenger impatience and rage.

questions.q: What shared structural feature do the P&G and Hong Kong bus cases illustrate?
options: Both involve criminal charges brought by law enforcement
Both involve companies breaking international trade laws
Both involve decisions with significant impact on multiple stakeholders where legal compliance alone is insufficient as an ethical guide
Both involve failures of individual negligence rather than systemic issues
Both result in complete business shutdown
questions.explain: Both cases share the structure: decisions with significant impact on multiple stakeholders (持份者), where legal compliance alone is insufficient as an ethical guide. This illustrates why business ethics goes beyond mere law-following.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a defining feature of business ethics according to the WHAT scope?
options: Issues involving different demands from various stakeholders
Business decisions with significant social or environmental impacts
Situations where potential conflicts arise among different aspects
Purely technical product design decisions with no social impact
Scenarios requiring evaluation of competing stakeholder interests
questions.explain: Business ethics specifically addresses issues with stakeholder involvement and social/environmental impact. Purely technical decisions without stakeholder implications fall outside the scope of business ethics as defined in this course.

questions.q: According to the formal definition, which group is NOT explicitly listed as a stakeholder?
options: Creditors (債權人)
Employees (員工)
Competitors (競爭對手)
Suppliers (供應商)
Government agencies
questions.explain: The definition lists creditors, directors, employees, government/agencies, owners/shareholders, suppliers, unions, and communities. Competitors, while potentially affected by a firm's actions, are not included in the formal stakeholder definition used in this course.

questions.q: What is the core difference between the shareholder and stakeholder approaches regarding CSR spending?
options: Shareholder approach favors unlimited CSR spending; stakeholder approach opposes it
Shareholder approach views CSR as a distraction; stakeholder approach views it as an obligation
Both approaches view CSR identically but disagree on implementation
Shareholder approach originated in Europe; stakeholder approach in the U.S.
CSR spending is irrelevant to both approaches
questions.explain: The shareholder approach views CSR spending as diluting (分散) firms' attention; CSR is not firms' competence. The stakeholder approach believes firms should concern themselves with the wellbeing of all stakeholders, making CSR an obligation.

questions.q: Where did the shareholder approach to corporate purpose originate?
options: The United Kingdom
Canada
Germany
The United States
Japan
questions.explain: The shareholder approach originated in the U.S., while the stakeholder approach is prevalent in Europe. This geographic distinction is a key differentiator between the two worldviews.

questions.q: Which teaching approach is used in MGMT 2130?
options: Lecture-only with no student interaction
Dilemmatic scenarios discussed in class with reflection, aimed at developing awareness and mindset
Rigid application of ethical frameworks to predetermined problems
Online simulation with no in-class discussion
Memorization of ethical codes and compliance rules
questions.explain: The teaching method uses dilemmatic scenarios (兩難情境) discussed in class with no single correct answer, mindful observation, and reflection. The goal is to develop awareness (意識), perspectives (視角), and mindset — not academic frameworks.

questions.q: What is the relationship between course pedagogy and course outcome in MGMT 2130?
options: Pedagogy teaches frameworks; outcome is formula-based answers
Pedagogy develops dilemmatic thinking; outcome is awareness and mindset rather than mechanical application
Pedagogy is purely theoretical; outcome is purely practical
Pedagogy focuses on lectures; outcome focuses on exams only
There is no connection between teaching method and course goals
questions.explain: The exam trap is that the course does NOT teach a single mechanical ethical framework. Pedagogy and outcome are aligned: discussion-based learning develops awareness and perspectives, not formula-based answers.

questions.q: How many class meetings does MGMT 2130 include in total?
options: 8 sessions
10 sessions
12 sessions
15 sessions
20 sessions
questions.explain: The course structure includes 12 class meetings total. Sessions 11 and 12 are dedicated to group presentations, while earlier sessions cover foundations, stakeholder relationships, and strategies.

questions.q: What are the three broad phases of MGMT 2130's curriculum?
options: Lecture, discussion, and exam
Ethical frameworks, case studies, and simulations
Foundations, Stakeholders, and Strategies
Individual projects, group work, and presentations
Theory, application, and assessment
questions.explain: The three phases are: (1) Foundations: Introduction and Psychology of Corporate (Ir)responsibility; (2) Stakeholders: Business and Employees, Customers, Suppliers, Communities, Natural Environment; (3) Strategies: Strategy and Innovation for Sustainability, Implementing Sustainability Strategy.

questions.q: Which resource is NOT available for MGMT 2130 students?
options: Internet resources via Canvas
Class notes downloadable from platform
Recommended textbook chapters
News, videos, and articles
Instructor-provided study guides
questions.explain: The course explicitly states 'No textbook; internet resources via Canvas; class notes downloadable; news, videos, articles.' There is no required or recommended textbook; learning relies on Canvas resources, notes, and multimedia materials.

questions.q: What is the combined weight of attendance and participation in the MGMT 2130 assessment?
questions.explain: Attendance and participation is weighted at 15% of the final grade. This breaks down into 5% attendance and 10% participation, making interpersonal engagement a significant component.

questions.q: Which assessment task carries the heaviest individual weight in MGMT 2130?
options: Attendance and participation (15%)
In-course case analysis (20%)
Simulation game (15%)
Group project (25%)
Final examination (25%)
questions.explain: Both the group project and final examination are weighted at 25% each, making them jointly the heaviest individual components. The group project involves analyzing a HKEX-listed firm's sustainability strategy.

questions.q: What is required on a participation card for grading memory?
options: Student name and date only
The main speaking point for the contribution
A summary of the entire class discussion
Proof of attendance and timestamp
A written essay on the topic
questions.explain: Each of the 5 participation cards must state the main speaking point for grading memory. This requirement ensures students articulate their contribution and allows the instructor to assess the quality of their involvement.

questions.q: According to the participation rubric, what score indicates 'offers straightforward information from material without elaboration'?
questions.explain: A score of 2 indicates 'offers straightforward information from material without elaboration; sporadic involvement; contributes moderately when called on.' This represents moderate participation without deep analysis or synthesis.

questions.q: What is the primary role assigned to students in the group project?
options: Academic researchers writing a peer-reviewed paper
Business consultants reviewing a firm's sustainability strategy
Government auditors enforcing compliance
Journalists investigating corporate fraud
Union representatives negotiating contracts
questions.explain: Students take the role of business consultants (商業顧問) reviewing a firm's sustainability strategy (可持續發展策略). The three guiding questions address industry challenges, current measures, and future recommendations.

questions.q: Which requirement must be met when selecting a company for the group project?
options: The firm must be a multinational corporation with over 10,000 employees
The firm must be listed on HKEX (香港交易所)
The firm must operate exclusively in Hong Kong
The firm must be a publicly traded U.S. company
The firm must have published a corporate governance report
questions.explain: The project requirement explicitly states the firm 'must be listed on HKEX (香港交易所).' This constrains the project to Hong Kong-traded companies, likely to ground the analysis in locally relevant sustainability issues.

questions.q: How long is the group project presentation, including Q&A?
options: 5 minutes total
10 minutes presentation with 3–5 minutes Q&A
15 minutes presentation with 10 minutes Q&A
20 minutes total
30 minutes total
questions.explain: The presentation format is 10-minute oral with 3–5 minute Q&A open to the whole class. Peer review (同儕評審) is conducted, and sequence is determined by lucky draw.

questions.q: What is the format of the final examination in MGMT 2130?
options: Multiple-choice only
Open-ended questions only
Multiple-choice and open-ended questions
Take-home essay
Oral presentation
questions.explain: The final exam includes both multiple-choice questions (選擇題) and open-ended questions (開放式題目). Details about content coverage are confirmed later in the course.

questions.q: On what date is the in-course case analysis administered?
options: March 12, 2026
March 26, 2026
April 9, 2026
April 23, 2026
questions.explain: The in-course case analysis is distributed and administered on March 26, 2026. It is a closed-book (閉卷) assessment lasting 1.5 hours with 3 questions to answer.

questions.q: What is the time limit for the in-course case analysis?
options: 1 hour
1.5 hours
2 hours
2.5 hours
3 hours
questions.explain: The in-course case analysis provides 1.5 hours total for students to answer 3 questions on a mini case distributed in class. It is a closed-book examination, so no external references are permitted.

questions.q: What preparation is required for the simulation game in MGMT 2130?
options: No preparation; students participate spontaneously on the day
Pre-familiarization with materials required; students must register on the website beforehand
Students must submit a written proposal one week before
Attendance at a mandatory preparatory workshop
Students must form groups and schedule practice sessions
questions.explain: Students must pre-familiarize themselves with materials and register on the website beforehand. The game is played in groups in class on April 23 and is graded on speed of task completion.

questions.q: On what date is the simulation game scheduled in MGMT 2130?
options: March 26, 2026
April 9, 2026
April 23, 2026
questions.explain: The simulation game (模擬遊戲) is played in groups in class on April 23, 2026. Grading is based on the speed of task completion, and pre-registration is required.

questions.q: What principle distinguishes the shareholder approach's view of corporate responsibility from the stakeholder approach?
options: Shareholder approach includes all affected parties; stakeholder approach focuses on profit alone
Shareholder approach prioritizes profit-maximization; stakeholder approach views firms as part of society responsible to all stakeholders
Both approaches are identical in practice but use different terminology
Shareholder approach is more recent than stakeholder approach
Stakeholder approach originated in the U.S.; shareholder approach in Europe
questions.explain: The core distinction is purpose: shareholders view profit-driving as the firm's nature and maximize shareholder value; stakeholders believe firms go beyond profit and are part of society. This fundamental difference shapes views on CSR, employee relations, and environmental responsibility.

questions.q: How do the P&G and bus cases together illustrate the relationship between legality and ethics?
options: Both show that legal actions are always ethical
Both demonstrate that legality and ethics are separate; legal actions can still raise ethical concerns
Both prove that ethical decisions are always more profitable
Both indicate that ethics should override all legal requirements
Both show that only illegal actions raise ethical questions
questions.explain: The P&G case shows dumpster diving was legal yet ethically contested; the bus case explores responsibility beyond driver negligence. Together, they illustrate that legality (合法性) and ethics (倫理) are distinct — one can be legal and still unethical, a core course theme.

questions.q: What is time perspective in psychological terms?
options: Age-based predisposition to view the future
Cognitive partitioning of experience into past, present, and future
Cultural framework inherited from family upbringing
Innate personality trait determined at birth
Training method for teaching emotional regulation
questions.explain: Time perspective is defined as a cognitive dimension that emerges from cognitive processes partitioning human experience into past, present, and future. It is not fixed by age or culture — it varies between individuals and can shift situationally (e.g. under competitive pressure).

questions.q: The Marshmallow Experiment demonstrates which concept?
options: Emotional intelligence in young children
Delayed gratification and future-oriented thinking
The role of reward in behavioral conditioning
Cultural differences in patience across societies
Genetic predisposition to self-control
questions.explain: The Marshmallow Experiment shows that children who resist eating one marshmallow immediately to receive two later demonstrate delayed gratification, illustrating that future-oriented thinking predicts better long-term outcomes.

questions.q: According to the lecture, happiness consists of two components. Which pairing correctly maps happiness components to time horizons?
options: Pleasure (future benefit) and Meaning (present benefit)
Pleasure (present benefit) and Meaning (future benefit)
Pleasure (past benefit) and Meaning (present benefit)
Pleasure (sustained benefit) and Meaning (cultural benefit)
Pleasure (emotional benefit) and Meaning (financial benefit)
questions.explain: The lecture defines Pleasure as present benefit (current enjoyment, e.g. eating pizza) and Meaning as future benefit (sense of purpose, e.g. having goals to run for). This distinction maps happiness to time horizons.

questions.q: What is the Zimbardo Time Perspective Inventory (ZTPI)?
options: A personality test measuring emotional stability
A standardized tool for measuring individual time orientation across multiple dimensions
A clinical assessment for diagnosing time-related disorders
An educational inventory for teaching future planning skills
A cultural assessment framework for cross-national research
questions.explain: The ZTPI is a standardized tool for measuring an individual's time orientation across dimensions such as past-negative, past-positive, present-hedonistic, present-fatalistic, and future.

questions.q: In Philip Zimbardo's view, what constitutes optimal time perspective for well-being?
options: Future-focused with minimal attention to the present
Balanced perspective drawing on positive past, moderate present enjoyment, and future planning
Present-focused with occasional planning for the future
Equal weight to all three time dimensions regardless of context
Past-focused with lessons learned driving all decisions
questions.explain: Zimbardo's "Time Paradox" argues that a balanced time perspective — combining positive memories, moderate present enjoyment, and future planning — is optimal for well-being and ethical decision making.

questions.q: How does the lecture explain VW engineers' decision to install defeat software using time perspective theory?
options: Engineers had no awareness of emissions standards
Engineers' time perspectives were unbalanced, narrowly focused on short-term gain (meeting targets) rather than long-term consequences
Engineers deliberately prioritized environmental damage for profit
Engineers believed the software would genuinely reduce emissions
Engineers were coerced by competitors into the decision
questions.explain: The lecture applies time perspective to explain the scandal: engineers had a narrow focus on short-term gain (meeting emissions targets quickly) rather than long-term consequences (reputational and legal damage).

questions.q: Which award did the 2009 VW Jetta TDI receive?
options: Motor Trend Car of the Year
Green Car of the Year from Green Car Journal
Best Diesel Engine Award from SAE International
Top Environmental Innovation Prize
Automotive Excellence Award for Clean Technology
questions.explain: The 2009 Jetta TDI was awarded Green Car of the Year by Green Car Journal for its apparent "groundbreaking clean diesel" engine that appeared to meet US emissions standards.

questions.q: What role did Ferdinand Piech play in the Volkswagen scandal?
options: He exposed the fraud to regulators
He was the engineer who designed the defeat software
He was identified as the man most responsible for VW's modern culture and direction
He was the CEO who managed the cover-up
He was the board member who approved emissions testing procedures
questions.explain: The lecture identifies Ferdinand Piech as the person most responsible for VW's modern culture and direction, highlighting his role in shaping the organization's decision-making environment.

questions.q: What technical fact about VW's options makes the decision to cheat a deliberate choice rather than a necessity?
options: VW lacked the engineering talent to develop clean diesel
VW had access to Daimler's alternative clean diesel solution but chose not to adopt it
VW did not have the financial resources to invest in new technology
VW's engines were physically incapable of meeting standards
VW's competitors had already developed similar defeat devices
questions.explain: VW had access to rival (Daimler's) alternative clean diesel solution yet chose not to adopt it, making the decision to install defeat software a deliberate choice rather than a technical constraint.

questions.q: Which CEO claim raised questions about leadership accountability in the VW scandal?
options: He claimed the scandal was a deliberate strategic test
He stated he was unaware of the engineers' decision to install defeat software
He blamed regulators for insufficient oversight
He claimed the defeat device was temporary and would be removed
He stated the decision was made before his tenure
questions.explain: CEO Martin Winterkorn stated he was unaware of the engineers' decision, raising questions about leadership accountability and organizational oversight.

questions.q: According to VW's Code of Conduct, which TWO corporate principles were explicitly stated?
options: Environmental responsibility and worker safety
Legal compliance and environmental responsibility
Profit maximization and legal compliance
Competitive advantage and sustainability
Transparency and innovation
questions.explain: VW's Code of Conduct explicitly stated: (1) Legal compliance — "We make no compromises on that," and (2) Environmental responsibility — "We bear responsibility for environmental compatibility and sustainability of our products."

questions.q: What key insight does McCoy's "Parable of the Sadhu" provide about organizational values?
options: Written codes are the most effective way to ensure ethical behavior
True organizational values are revealed under stress, not in printed codes; stories people tell transmit actual behavioral norms
Organizations need stronger enforcement mechanisms for code violations
Ethical behavior is determined by individual conscience rather than organizational culture
External audits are the best way to ensure compliance
questions.explain: McCoy's parable illustrates that true organizational values (真正的組織價值觀) are revealed under stress, not in printed documents. Stories people tell — not formal codes — transmit actual conceptions of proper behavior.

questions.q: How does the VW scandal exemplify the difference between stated and actual organizational values?
options: VW lacked any written code of conduct to begin with
VW had a detailed Code of Conduct that explicitly prohibited emissions violations, yet the scandal shows it was disregarded under pressure
VW's actual values aligned perfectly with the code, making the scandal an individual failure
The scandal proves that codes are unimportant to modern organizations
VW's code was too recent to be implemented effectively
questions.explain: The VW scandal is a direct example of a company with a detailed written code that was nonetheless violated. This demonstrates that codes are necessary but not sufficient for ensuring ethical behavior.

questions.q: Define groupthink according to the lecture.
options: When a group collectively decides to commit fraud
When group members strive to agree for unanimity at the expense of accurate information assessment
When group leaders suppress dissent through authoritarian control
When individuals in a group lose their personal identity
When a group abandons rational decision-making processes
questions.explain: Groupthink occurs when group members strive to agree for the sake of unanimity and thus at the expense of accurate assessment of information relevant to a decision.

questions.q: Which of the following is an ADVANTAGE of group decision making?
options: Elimination of individual cognitive biases
Greater pool of knowledge (Wisdom of the crowds)
Faster decision-making compared to individual decisions
Complete elimination of groupthink risks
Reduced need for organizational accountability
questions.explain: Group decision making has advantages including greater pool of knowledge (Wisdom of the crowds), intellectual stimulation, and greater commitment to decisions.

questions.q: Which of the following is a DISADVANTAGE of group decision making?
options: Reduced diversity of perspectives
Problematic group dynamics and diffusion of responsibility
Elimination of all conflict
Faster time to implementation
Increased individual accountability
questions.explain: Disadvantages of group decision making include problematic group dynamics (groupthink), time consumption, and diffusion of responsibility.

questions.q: Which of the following is a symptom of groupthink?
options: Diverse perspectives actively encouraged
Illusion of invulnerability — group members discount negative information believing the group cannot fail
Critical evaluation of all alternative solutions
Transparent dissent and open disagreement
Regular revision of the group's position based on new evidence
questions.explain: Illusion of invulnerability is a key symptom where group members discount negative information or warnings, believing the group cannot fail.

questions.q: What does self-censorship mean in the context of groupthink?
options: The organization censors members' communications externally
Members restrain themselves from expressing ideas that deviate from group consensus
Leaders silence dissenting voices through formal processes
The group collectively censors external criticism
Members are prevented from attending group meetings
questions.explain: Self-censorship (自我審查) means members restrain themselves from expressing ideas that deviate from the group consensus, reducing the expression of alternative viewpoints.

questions.q: How is the illusion of unanimity created in groupthink?
options: Explicit voting procedures enforce agreement
Silence by a member is interpreted as consent, creating a false impression that all agree
Leaders announce consensus without member input
Majority rules force the minority to conform
All members must verbally affirm the decision
questions.explain: The illusion of unanimity occurs when silence by a member is interpreted as consent, creating a false impression that all members agree with the group decision.

questions.q: Which exam trap relates to diffusion of responsibility?
options: It is one of the four named symptoms of groupthink
It is a disadvantage of group decision making, not one of the four named symptoms of groupthink
It is a benefit of collaborative work
It only occurs in organizational hierarchies
It is synonymous with peer pressure
questions.explain: An important exam trap: "Diffusion of responsibility" is a disadvantage of group decision making, not one of the four named symptoms of groupthink. The four symptoms are illusion of invulnerability, peer pressure, self-censorship, and illusion of unanimity.

questions.q: According to the lecture, how can organizations avoid groupthink?
options: Eliminate all group decision-making processes
Critically identify and evaluate all reasons the preferred alternative might be unacceptable before committing
Appoint one authoritarian leader to make decisions
Suppress dissenting opinions early in the process
Avoid diverse membership in decision-making groups
questions.explain: Groupthink avoidance strategy: critically identify and evaluate all reasons that might make the "preferred" alternative unacceptable before committing to it.

questions.q: What real-world example does the lecture use to illustrate groupthink failure?
options: The Enron accounting scandal
The Challenger space shuttle launch decision where dissenting engineers' warnings were suppressed
The 2008 financial crisis
The Theranos fraud case
The Cambridge Analytica data breach
questions.explain: The lecture cites the Challenger space shuttle launch decision as a classic groupthink failure where dissenting engineers' warnings were suppressed under schedule and authority pressure.

questions.q: How does the lecture explain two unsolved puzzles about the VW scandal using groupthink?
options: Incompetent engineers and weak corporate leadership
Why engineers colluded on massive deception AND why nobody stood up to stop the obvious wrongdoing are both consistent with groupthink dynamics
Regulatory failure and government negligence
Market competition and profit pressures alone
Technical misunderstandings and poor communication
questions.explain: The lecture applies groupthink theory to explain both why VW engineers colluded on such massive deception and why nobody stood up to stop the obvious wrongdoing.

questions.q: What does John C. Maxwell's framework identify as drivers of unethical corporate decisions?
options: Lack of regulatory oversight and market pressure
Inadequate training and poor communication
Five psychological drivers: Pleasure, Power, Pride, Priorities, and Pressure
Systemic organizational failures and weak governance
Individual incompetence and lack of experience
questions.explain: Maxwell's framework identifies five psychological drivers (心理驅動因素) that lead otherwise good managers toward unethical corporate decisions: Pleasure, Power, Pride, Priorities, and Pressure.

questions.q: Which of the 5 Ps refers to short-term benefits and material gain?
options: Power
Pleasure — short-term benefits; "quick money" for material life
Pride
Priorities
Pressure
questions.explain: Pleasure (享樂) in Maxwell's framework refers to short-term benefits and "quick money" for material life.

questions.q: What does the "Pride" driver in Maxwell's framework relate to?
options: Legitimate desire for professional achievement
"Ego"; protective obsession with self and image; initial high promise creates pressure to maintain reputation
Confidence in one's decision-making abilities
Assertiveness in organizational settings
Commitment to company values
questions.explain: Pride (自尊/驕傲) refers to ego and protective obsession with self and image; high initial promise creates pressure to maintain reputation, often leading to defensive or unethical behavior.

questions.q: How do "Priorities" as a psychological driver contribute to unethical decisions?
options: Individuals prioritize personal goals over company goals
Core values are misaligned; inadequate consideration of stakeholders' interests
Decision-makers prioritize speed over quality
Teams prioritize consensus over accuracy
Organizations prioritize profit over all other metrics
questions.explain: Priorities (優先順序) as a driver refers to core values being misaligned and inadequate consideration of stakeholders' interests, leading to decisions that harm broader constituencies.

questions.q: Which driver in the 5 Ps framework directly addresses time constraints and competition?
options: Pleasure
Power
Pride
Pressure — competition, peer pressure, authority figures, and time constraints driving rushed decisions
Priorities
questions.explain: Pressure (壓力) refers to competition, peer pressure, authority figures, and time constraints driving rushed decisions that may bypass ethical consideration.

questions.q: How do the 5 Ps differ from organizational or systemic explanations of unethical behavior?
options: The 5 Ps ignore individual motivation entirely
The 5 Ps are organizational-level factors while systemic causes are individual-level
The 5 Ps explain individual manager decisions; they do not address organizational-level causes like weak governance or regulatory gaps
The 5 Ps are more accurate than systemic explanations
There is no meaningful distinction between the two types of explanation
questions.explain: An exam trap: All five Ps are psychological/individual-level factors. They explain the individual manager's decision, not organizational system failures. Weak governance structures and regulatory gaps are separate, systemic explanations.

questions.q: What does Dan Ariely's research on moral code suggest about human ethical behavior?
options: Humans are naturally highly ethical without external incentives
Human moral reasoning is "buggy": people overestimate their own ethical behavior and underestimate situational triggers for cheating
Ethics are primarily determined by cultural background
Moral behavior improves consistently as people age and gain experience
Individual morality is unchangeable regardless of context
questions.explain: Ariely's research shows that human moral reasoning is "buggy" — people consistently overestimate their own ethical behavior and underestimate how situational triggers can lead to cheating.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four core consumer rights?
options: Right to be refunded unconditionally
Right to choose
Right to be safe
Right to be heard
Right to be informed
questions.explain: The four core consumer rights are choose, safe, informed, and heard. While refunds may be part of seeking redress (補救), the right itself is 'to be heard' (申訴權), not an automatic refund. This exam trap catches students who conflate redress procedures with a blanket refund right.

questions.q: What does the 'right to be heard' (申訴權) specifically protect?
options: Freedom to speak during shopping
Access to complaint channels and redress mechanisms
The right to negotiate product prices
Immunity from any negative feedback
Priority access to new product launches
questions.explain: The right to be heard (申訴權) ensures consumers have appropriate methods for addressing conflict and seeking redress (補救), not mere freedom of speech or price negotiation rights.

questions.q: Which of the following violations represents a breach of the 'right to be informed' (知情權)?
options: A restaurant fails to display the menu in the window
A supermarket uses misleading price comparison tricks on promotional goods
A gym closes without advance notice
A store sells products past the expiration date
A retailer offers discounts without advertising them
questions.explain: The Consumer Council in Hong Kong flagged supermarkets using misleading price comparison tricks as violating the right to be informed (知情權) — customers must receive truthful, full disclosure (披露) of product information.

questions.q: What enforcement action did Hong Kong Customs take regarding short-weight (缺斤少両) practices?
options: Closed all affected outlets permanently
Imposed fines without warnings
Issued citations at approximately 100 outlets including restaurants and seafood stalls
Required mandatory re-training of all staff
Established a public black-list of violators
questions.explain: Customs uncovered short-weight malpractices at roughly 100 outlets across restaurants, seafood stalls, and fruit stands, demonstrating systemic enforcement of consumer protection standards.

questions.q: Why did the Hong Kong gym imprisonment case represent a landmark in consumer protection law?
options: It was the first time a gym was required to refund all memberships
It marked the first imprisonment under Hong Kong's sales law for trapping students into memberships
It established new legal protections for university students only
It set a precedent for banning all fitness industry marketing
It was the longest consumer protection trial in Hong Kong history
questions.explain: This was the first imprisonment under Hong Kong sales law (銷售法) for trapping students into health club memberships, marking a significant enforcement escalation from fines to criminal penalties.

questions.q: According to the ICC Advertising and Marketing Communications Code, which of these is NOT a required standard for marketing communication?
options: Legal (合法)
Honest (誠實)
Profitable (盈利)
Decent (得體)
Truthful (真實)
questions.explain: The four required standards are legal, decent, honest, and truthful. Profitability is a business goal but not an ethical standard under the ICC Code.

questions.q: What does the ICC Code require regarding a company's exploitation of consumer knowledge gaps?
options: It encourages companies to maximize information asymmetry
It permits exploitation in developing markets but not developed ones
It allows exploitation only if products are clearly labeled
It prohibits companies from exploiting consumers' lack of experience or knowledge
It requires explicit disclosure of knowledge gaps before purchase
questions.explain: The ICC Code explicitly states that marketing must not abuse consumers' trust (信任) or exploit their lack of experience or knowledge. This protects vulnerable consumers from predatory practices.

questions.q: How does the lecture frame self-regulation (自律) as distinct from mandatory regulation?
options: Self-regulation is always more effective than government rules
Self-regulation primarily benefits government agencies
Self-regulation eliminates the need for legal compliance
Self-regulation applies only to large multinational corporations
Self-regulation can serve as a competitive differentiator (競爭差異化) in privacy-focused markets
questions.explain: The lecture frames self-regulation as a business opportunity — companies like DuckDuckGo and Proton use privacy protection as a revenue-generating competitive advantage, not just a cost of compliance.

questions.q: Which of the following companies was cited as an example of privacy-focused self-regulation?
options: Google Chrome
Facebook Messenger
ProtonMail
TikTok
Amazon Web Services
questions.explain: ProtonMail is Swiss-based, ad-free, and offers end-to-end encryption (端對端加密) as a privacy-first business model. Google Chrome, Facebook, TikTok, and AWS all collect user data as part of their business models.

questions.q: What key feature distinguishes Tresorit from other cloud storage providers in its privacy approach?
options: It stores files only within European Union servers
It offers end-to-end encryption (端對端加密) for all files
It charges premium prices to fund security research
It requires government approval before processing data
It encrypts data only during transmission, not at rest
questions.explain: Tresorit uses end-to-end encryption (端對端加密) as its privacy mechanism, meaning only the user holds decryption keys — even Tresorit cannot access the stored files.

questions.q: According to the crisis statistics presented, what is the relationship between crisis incidence and crisis preparedness?
options: More businesses have experienced a crisis (59%) than have a plan for one (54%)
More businesses have crisis plans (59%) than have experienced a crisis (54%)
Exactly equal numbers have experienced crises and have plans for them
Most small businesses have plans while large ones lack preparedness
Crisis preparedness precedes crisis experience
questions.explain: The counterintuitive finding is that 59% have experienced a crisis, yet only 54% have a crisis response plan (危機應對計劃). This means ~5% of businesses face crises without prior planning.

questions.q: What is the projected customer impact of a single negative search result appearing on the first page?
options: Loss of 5% of potential customers
Loss of 15% of potential customers
Loss of 22% of potential customers
Loss of 40% of potential customers
Loss of 50% of potential customers
questions.explain: One negative article (負面文章) on the first page of search results can cost a business 22% of its customers — illustrating the severe reputational damage from unchecked crisis narratives.

questions.q: In the Haidilao hygiene crisis (衛生危機), what specific cleanliness violations were discovered in August 2017?
options: Expired ingredients in the storage freezer
Rats found in the kitchen and a dustpan (畚箕) being used to wash plates
Inadequate hand-washing facilities
Live insects in the dining area
Mold growth in the ventilation system
questions.explain: On August 25, 2017, news broke that rats were found in the kitchen and a dustpan (畚箕) intended for cleaning was being used to wash plates — severe hygiene breaches.

questions.q: What reputation did Haidilao have prior to its hygiene crisis?
options: It was China's newest hotpot chain with limited customer base
It was known for exceptional customer service (顧客服務) and employee welfare (員工福利)
It was a budget fast-food chain focused on speed
It was a Western restaurant struggling to compete
It had been the subject of previous food safety recalls
questions.explain: Haidilao is China's best-known hotpot (火鍋) chain — renowned for exceptional customer service and employee welfare, which made the hygiene crisis especially damaging to its brand image.

questions.q: How quickly did Haidilao respond to the hygiene crisis with official communication?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 7 hours with 2 public statements (公開聲明)
Within 48 hours
Within 3 days
Within 1 week
questions.explain: The company issued 2 public statements (公開聲明) within 7 hours of the crisis breaking, demonstrating rapid response aligned with the 'Control' principle in crisis management.

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT part of Haidilao's crisis response (危機回應)?
options: Admitted management fault for the lapses (失誤)
Shut down implicated branches immediately
Refused to cooperate with media investigations
Engaged third-party pest controllers (第三方害蟲防治公司)
Extended checks to overseas branches (海外分店)
questions.explain: Haidilao actually welcomed monitoring (監察) by customers, media, and government — refusing media cooperation was the opposite of their transparent crisis response strategy.

questions.q: What distinctive transparency measure did Haidilao take when reopening affected branches?
options: Hired external auditors to inspect daily operations
Posted anonymous customer reviews on the website
Installed livestreaming (直播) from the kitchen to demonstrate transparency (透明度)
Released detailed medical reports on all staff
Reduced prices to regain customer trust
questions.explain: Haidilao reopened branches with livestreaming (直播) from the kitchen, demonstrating transparency (透明度) in real-time — a modern approach to crisis recovery.

questions.q: What role did Haidilao's board of directors (董事會) take during the crisis response?
options: They delegated all responsibility to front-line managers
They maintained a public silence to avoid legal liability
They demanded the CEO's immediate resignation
They shouldered key responsibilities, reassuring employees not to panic
They filed for bankruptcy protection
questions.explain: The board of directors (董事會) shouldered key responsibilities and assured affected employees not to panic, demonstrating top-level accountability and leadership during the crisis.

questions.q: Of the three Cs in crisis management (Care, Communication, Control), which one focuses on demonstrating concern for public interests beyond legal compliance?
options: Communication (溝通)
Care (關懷)
Control (控制)
Compliance (合規)
Credibility (公信力)
questions.explain: Care (關懷) specifically demonstrates that the company cares about the public's interests or problems — going beyond mere legal compliance to show genuine concern.

questions.q: What is the primary function of 'Communication' (溝通) within the three Cs of crisis management?
options: Simply talking more frequently about the crisis
Consolidating channels to ensure timely (及時) and accurate (準確) messaging
Avoiding all public statements until the crisis passes
Using only social media for official announcements
Hiring external PR firms to shift blame
questions.explain: Communication (溝通) means consolidating communication channels (溝通渠道) for speed and accuracy — maintaining control of the crisis narrative (危機敘述), not merely increasing communication frequency.

questions.q: Why is 'Control' (控制) critical in crisis management, according to the lecture?
options: To prevent any criticism from external parties
To allow the company to deny responsibility completely
To respond quickly and maintain some control of crisis development (危機發展), preventing external parties from entirely setting the narrative
To minimize employee involvement in crisis response
To eliminate the need for transparency
questions.explain: Control (控制) means responding quickly to maintain some control of crisis development (危機發展) — preventing the narrative from being set entirely by external parties. It's not about denying responsibility but about active, swift response.

questions.q: Which of the following is a required element of a perfect corporate apology (完整企業道歉)?
options: Anonymity of the responsible parties
Silence about corrective measures
Well-timed (時機適當) issuance of the apology
Blame assignment to individual scapegoats
Promise of financial compensation without acknowledgment
questions.explain: A well-timed (時機適當) apology — issued promptly — is one of the five required elements. A delayed apology loses credibility (公信力), making timeliness essential.

questions.q: What specifically must be acknowledged in the first element of a perfect apology?
options: The company's financial losses
The specific wrongdoing that occurred
The customer's emotional reaction
Industry best practices
Regulatory requirements
questions.explain: The first element — Acknowledges the mistake or wrongdoing (承認錯誤) — requires stating specifically what went wrong, not general statements about the impact.

questions.q: An apology that only expresses regret but does NOT accept responsibility would be considered:
options: A perfect apology with one element emphasized
An incomplete apology lacking one essential element
A legally sufficient apology
A strategic apology for future reference
An appropriate interim response
questions.explain: The second element — Accepts responsibility (接受責任) — is distinct from expressing regret. Missing either element weakens credibility and effectiveness; all five are required for a perfect apology.

questions.q: What psychological barrier does the VW emissions scandal (大眾汽車排放醜聞) illustrate regarding crisis admission?
options: Employees refuse to report problems to management
Leaders often lack the courage (勇氣) to admit mistakes, even when cover-ups (掩蓋) worsen outcomes
Customers never believe corporate apologies
Media always amplifies corporate statements
Regulators deliberately delay enforcement
questions.explain: The VW case demonstrates why leaders sometimes choose cover-up (掩蓋) over admission — key question is why people lack the courage (勇氣) to acknowledge mistakes despite worse long-term consequences.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a psychological factor driving cover-up (掩蓋) behavior in the VW scandal analysis?
options: Fear of legal liability (法律責任)
Reputational loss (聲譽損失)
Concern for employee morale
Sunk-cost reasoning (沉沒成本思維)
Fear of market competition
questions.explain: The lecture identifies three psychological factors: fear of legal liability (法律責任), reputational loss (聲譽損失), and sunk-cost reasoning (沉沒成本思維). Market competition concerns are not mentioned as a primary psychological driver.

questions.q: How do the Haidilao case and the VW scandal illustrate opposite approaches to crisis management?
options: Both companies denied wrongdoing completely
Neither company issued formal apologies
Both companies avoided public communication
VW handled the crisis better than Haidilao
Haidilao admitted fault and took action quickly; VW initially chose denial and cover-up (掩蓋)
questions.explain: Haidilao's rapid admission, transparency, and action contrasts sharply with VW's initial denial and concealment, demonstrating that courage to admit mistakes early can preserve reputation better than cover-ups.

questions.q: Which combination of crisis management principles (Care, Communication, Control) did Haidilao exemplify most clearly?
options: Only Communication
Only Control
Care, Communication, and Control — showing concern for public interests, rapid messaging consolidation, and quick narrative management
Only Care
None of the above
questions.explain: Haidilao demonstrated all three Cs: Care (taking responsibility for public safety), Communication (2 statements in 7 hours, consolidating messaging), and Control (quick action and livestreaming to shape the recovery narrative).

questions.q: Why does the lecture emphasize that treating customers ethically is a 'strategic asset' rather than just a legal requirement?
options: Ethics improve government approval ratings
Strategic ethics eliminate the need for product quality
The Haidilao case shows that transparent, rapid, and accountable crisis management can strengthen a brand
Legal compliance alone guarantees customer loyalty
Strategic assets reduce the need for customer service
questions.explain: The lecture's throughline is that ethical treatment of customers — as exemplified by Haidilao's crisis response — is not just legally necessary but strategically valuable for brand strength and customer retention.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the core distinction between DuckDuckGo, Brave, and ProtonMail as discussed in the lecture?
options: They are the cheapest options available in their categories
They compete on price rather than quality or privacy
They are required by law to operate with strict privacy standards
They offer anonymous browsing and encrypted communication to differentiate from mainstream competitors
They receive government subsidies for their privacy features
questions.explain: These companies illustrate self-regulation (自律) as a competitive differentiator (競爭差異化) — they proactively build privacy protections into their business models to compete in the market, rather than being forced by regulation.

questions.q: According to Barry Schwartz, what creates a self-fulfilling cycle in workplace motivation?
options: Assuming workers are money-motivated, then stripping autonomy, which makes workers actually money-motivated
Offering high salaries first, then expecting increased productivity
Hiring workers with strong personal values, then enforcing strict rules
Installing safety nets and offering bonuses without improving job design
Creating diverse teams and then implementing strict performance metrics
questions.explain: Schwartz identifies that organizations assume workers are money-motivated, which shapes job design toward control and measurement. This design strips work of autonomy and meaning, which in turn makes workers focus only on money — confirming the original assumption. The other options misrepresent the lecture's key mechanism about how assumptions shape outcomes.

questions.q: What is the Career Sweet Spot?
options: The highest salary a person can earn in their industry
The intersection of Reward (might do), Strength (can do), and Passion (want to do)
The point at which you have worked for five years or more
The role where you spend the least amount of time on administrative tasks
The moment you receive your first promotion at a company
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly defines the Career Sweet Spot as the intersection of three overlapping dimensions: what others will pay you for (Reward), what uses your gifts (Strength), and what emotionally engages you (Passion). Having only one or two dimensions does not produce the sweet spot.

questions.q: Sean Aiken's year-long "One Week Job" experiment revealed that happiness at work depends most on which two factors?
options: High salary and job security
Flexible hours and remote work options
The people you work with and feeling your work is significant
Career advancement opportunities and clear promotion pathways
Access to professional development and training programs
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that Sean Aiken's key insight from trying 52 jobs in 52 weeks was that finding one singular passion is not the key to happiness. Instead, two factors dominate: (1) the people you work with, and (2) the feeling that your work is significant.

questions.q: Which of the following describes why the Career Sweet Spot requires all three dimensions to overlap?
options: Having only passion without reward and strength will leave you fulfilled but underpaid
Having only strength and reward without passion means you can do it and get paid for it, but it won't ignite you emotionally
Having only passion means your work is emotionally engaging but you lack the skills or market value
Both B and C accurately describe incomplete combinations
The lecture does not address why all three are necessary; it only states they must overlap
questions.explain: The notes indicate that having only one or two dimensions produces an incomplete experience. Option B correctly identifies what happens without passion (competence and compensation without emotional engagement), and Option C correctly identifies what happens without strength and reward (emotional engagement without capability or market viability). Option A misrepresents the outcome — passion without the others leaves you unfulfilled, not fulfilled but underpaid.

questions.q: What does the Foxconn case illustrate about addressing workplace meaninglessness?
options: Raising salaries twice in three months is the most effective solution to employee dissatisfaction
Hiring sociologists and psychiatrists can fully resolve the problem of meaningless work
Addressing physical and financial symptoms without addressing meaninglessness is ethically insufficient
Safety nets and hotlines are the most direct way to restore employee engagement
Contractual pledges prevent employees from making harmful decisions
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly treats Foxconn's four responses (salary raises, pledges, safety nets, professional support) as evidence that addressing symptoms without addressing meaninglessness is ethically insufficient. The examination notes state that Foxconn's responses are often mistaken for adequate solutions, but the lecture frames them as inadequate.

questions.q: According to the lecture, why did Foxconn employees describe their work as meaningless?
options: They were underpaid and had no access to healthcare benefits
They repeated the same task daily, received harsh treatment, and saw no connection to a larger purpose
The company refused to hire workers with passion for technology
The work required constant learning and skill development that was exhausting
They had too much autonomy and lacked clear direction from management
questions.explain: The lecture quotes employees as saying: 'Life is meaningless. Everyday, I repeat the same thing I did yesterday. We get yelled at all the time. It's very tough around here.' This reflects repetition, harsh treatment, and the absence of meaning or impact — not pay issues, learning demands, or autonomy problems.

questions.q: What would be a meaningful structural change that Foxconn could make to address the root cause of employee meaninglessness?
options: Reduce working hours from 12 to 10 hours per day
Introduce craft identity, team belonging, or visible impact on the final product
Increase the frequency of salary reviews to quarterly
Install more entertainment facilities in the dormitory
Hire only workers who already have passion for electronics manufacturing
questions.explain: The lecture's discussion question explicitly asks: 'What meaning could Foxconn convincingly and realistically introduce?' and provides examples such as craft identity, team belonging, and visible impact on the final product. The other options address comfort or recruitment, not the root meaninglessness of repetitive assembly work.

questions.q: According to Martin Seligman's framework, which of the following best describes the "Pleasant Life"?
options: Engagement and absorption through flow state
Affiliation and sense of purpose beyond oneself
Enjoyment and pursuit of positive experiences and pleasure
Autonomy and control over one's daily schedule
Achievement of long-term career milestones
questions.explain: The lecture's table defines the Pleasant Life as pursuit of enjoyment and positive experiences. Option A describes the Good Life (engagement via flow), and Option B describes the Meaningful Life (affiliation and purpose). Options D and E are not part of Seligman's framework.

questions.q: Which of Seligman's three happy lives is most closely associated with the concept of flow?
options: The Pleasant Life
The Meaningful Life
The Good Life
The Balanced Life
The Achieved Life
questions.explain: The table explicitly pairs the Good Life with 'Engagement; absorption (投入) via flow state.' The Good Life is the path that depends on full engagement and the flow experience, unlike the Pleasant Life (enjoyment) or the Meaningful Life (purpose and affiliation).

questions.q: What are the three conditions that Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi identifies as necessary for flow to occur?
options: Reward, strength, and passion
Autonomy, relatedness, and competence
Clear goals, immediate feedback, and challenge level matching skill level
Purpose, engagement, and pleasure
Structure, support, and social connection
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly lists the three flow conditions: (1) Clear goals, (2) Immediate feedback, and (3) Challenge level matches skill level. Options A, B, D, and E refer to other frameworks or psychological constructs but are not the flow conditions Csikszentmihalyi identifies.

questions.q: According to the lecture, where does flow most commonly occur?
options: Only during leisure activities such as hobbies and sports
Primarily during vacations and time off
Surprisingly often at work, not just leisure, provided three conditions are met
Only for people with high-status or creative jobs
Never in routine-seeming roles, regardless of job design
questions.explain: The lecture states: 'Flow occurs surprisingly often at work — not just leisure — as long as three conditions are met.' This emphasizes that flow is not restricted to leisure and that even routine roles can enable flow if the conditions are present. Option E contradicts this claim.

questions.q: If a job has clear goals and immediate feedback but the challenge level is far below your current skill level, what is the likely result?
options: Flow state will occur because two of three conditions are met
Boredom rather than flow, because the third condition (challenge-skill match) is not met
The Good Life will be achieved through the Pleasant Life pathway
Immediate happiness will increase, though flow will not occur
The employee will become unmotivated and leave the job
questions.explain: Flow requires all three conditions: clear goals, immediate feedback, AND challenge matching skill. The lecture notes state: 'Work that provides these three conditions enables the Good Life; missing any one prevents the flow state.' If challenge is too low (below your skill), you experience boredom, not flow, even if the other two conditions are present.

questions.q: What does Shawn Achor claim about the relationship between happiness and performance?
options: Hard work leads to success, which eventually leads to happiness
Happiness and optimism fuel performance and achievement; happiness comes first
Performance and achievement are independent of emotional state
Happiness is the result of success, not the cause of it
Performance depends on salary and external rewards, not internal emotional state
questions.explain: The lecture directly states that Achor challenges the traditional formula (work hard → be successful → become happy) and argues it is 'backward.' His revised formula is: happiness and optimism fuel performance and achievement — happiness comes first. Option A represents the old formula, which Achor rejects.

questions.q: According to Achor's Happiness Advantage, what is the strategic implication for employers?
options: Creating conditions for employee happiness is a nice-to-have but not essential
Creating conditions for employee happiness is both strategically rational and ethically required
Happiness is a personal responsibility that employees must pursue on their own time
Employers should focus only on performance metrics, not employee well-being
Happiness programs are too expensive relative to their return on investment
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states: 'Implication for employers: creating conditions for employee happiness is not just compassionate, it is strategically rational and ethically required.' This connects happiness to both business performance and ethical duty, rejecting the view that happiness is peripheral or solely a personal matter.

questions.q: How does Achor characterize the phrase "happiness is a work ethic"?
options: Happiness is a reward that employees earn through hard work
Happiness should be treated as a professional discipline, not just a reward
Happiness requires employees to work longer hours without additional pay
Happiness is best pursued outside of work, not during the workday
Happiness is an optional luxury that only high-performing employees deserve
questions.explain: The lecture quotes Achor: '"Happiness is a work ethic" — treating positive emotions as a professional discipline, not a reward.' This frames happiness as an active practice and professional responsibility, not something passive or earned only as a reward.

questions.q: What are the employer duties identified in the lecture?
options: Provide competitive salaries and follow legal compliance requirements
Design work that enables meaning, flow, and autonomy; hire for values alignment; address well-being proactively
Hire the most talented workers regardless of their values or beliefs
Focus only on quarterly profits and shareholder returns
Limit employee autonomy to maintain control and predictability
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly lists employer duties as: (1) design work that enables meaning, flow, and autonomy, (2) hire for values alignment, not just skills, and (3) address well-being proactively (not reactively as Foxconn did). The other options contradict the lecture's values-based approach to employment.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what are the employee duties in the employer-employee relationship?
options: Work as much as possible to maximize company profits
Engage authentically, pursue the sweet spot, and take ownership of finding significance in their role
Follow all orders without question or personal consideration
Prioritize salary and benefits above all else
Avoid taking any personal responsibility for their work experience
questions.explain: The lecture states: 'Employee duties: engage authentically; pursue the sweet spot; take ownership of finding significance in their role.' This emphasizes active engagement and personal responsibility, balanced against the employer's duty to create conditions for meaning and flow.

questions.q: How does the lecture's personal reflection exercise ("Be the observer of your own decisions and feelings") support the employer-employee duties discussion?
options: It suggests employees should observe others' decisions rather than their own
It positions self-awareness as the starting point for both employers and employees to understand their roles and responsibilities
It implies employees should withdraw emotionally from their work
It suggests that feelings are unimportant in professional relationships
It is unrelated to the duties discussion and appears in a different section of the course
questions.explain: The lecture notes state: 'The personal reflection exercise reinforces that self-awareness is the starting point for both parties.' This connects the reflection practice to the employer-employee duties framework, suggesting that understanding one's own decisions and feelings enables authentic engagement and meaningful employer-employee relationships.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates Simon Sinek's principle about hiring for shared beliefs?
options: Hire workers purely based on technical skills and years of experience
Hire people who believe what you believe, so they will work with 'blood and sweat and tears,' not just for money
Hire workers who are most willing to prioritize salary and benefits
Hire workers who are indifferent to company values to avoid bias
Hire workers who are most skeptical of the company's mission
questions.explain: The lecture quotes Sinek: 'If you hire people just because they can do a job, they'll work for your money. But if you hire people who believe what you believe, they'll work for you with blood and sweat and tears.' This directly contrasts skill-based hiring with values-aligned hiring and their different outcomes.

questions.q: According to the lecture, why is the assumption that workers are money-motivated considered an ethical problem?
options: Because money is not actually important to workers
Because it ignores that how a firm structures work is a moral choice that affects employee dignity and well-being
Because it leads to higher wages, which is unfair to shareholders
Because money-motivated workers are less productive than passion-driven workers
Because most workers actually prefer to work without any compensation
questions.explain: The lecture notes state: 'The implication for business ethics: how a firm structures work is a moral choice, not just a management decision.' This frames the money-motivation assumption as an ethical issue because job design choices affect dignity and well-being. The lecture also notes in exam traps: 'In this course it is framed as an ethics question.'

questions.q: What is the main insight of the exam trap regarding the Career Sweet Spot?
options: The sweet spot is easy to find if you are passionate enough
The sweet spot can be achieved with just passion, without reward or strength
The sweet spot requires ALL three dimensions — passion alone is not sufficient
The sweet spot is different for each person and cannot be defined universally
The sweet spot is a myth created by career coaches to sell books
questions.explain: The exam trap explicitly states: 'The sweet spot requires ALL three dimensions — reward, strength, and passion. Having only passion (熱情) without the others is not the sweet spot.' This corrects the misconception that passion is sufficient alone.

questions.q: According to the Foxconn case discussion, who bears responsibility for introducing meaning into work?
options: Only the employees themselves; employers should not be responsible for employees' personal fulfillment
Primarily the employees, though employers can offer support services
This is the core ethical debate addressed in the lecture; the question is whether meaningful work is a right or a personal pursuit
Exclusively the government through labor regulations
Equally the workers and external therapists, but not the employer directly
questions.explain: The lecture notes state: 'The core ethical debate: is meaningful work a right, or a personal pursuit?' This is framed as a deliberate question the lecture raises, not a settled conclusion. The notes also discuss the concern about whether hiring for shared beliefs constitutes manipulation versus authentic alignment, reflecting the ethical complexity.

questions.q: How do the three happy lives differ in terms of their sustainability and quality according to the lecture?
options: All three are equally sustainable and provide the same quality of life
The Meaningful Life and Good Life are more sustainable than the Pleasant Life, which is based on transient experiences
The Pleasant Life is the most sustainable because pleasure is the easiest to obtain
The lecture does not address differences in sustainability or quality among the three lives
Only the Good Life is sustainable; the other two fade quickly
questions.explain: While the lecture does not explicitly rank them, it presents them as distinct paths with different 'quality and sustainability.' The table suggests that the Meaningful Life (purpose) and Good Life (flow/engagement) provide deeper, more durable satisfaction than the Pleasant Life (transient pleasure). The context implies qualitative differences in how fulfilling each path is.

questions.q: What does the lecture's examination of both Barry Schwartz and Simon Sinek suggest about the power of organizational assumptions?
options: Organizational assumptions have no effect on employee motivation or behavior
Assumptions shape job design, which in turn influences whether workers become money-motivated or values-aligned
Employees' beliefs are fixed and cannot be changed by organizational assumptions
Organizational assumptions are less important than market competition
The lecture addresses only Schwartz's view, not Sinek's perspective on assumptions
questions.explain: The lecture presents both thinkers as illustrating how organizational assumptions create self-reinforcing systems: Schwartz shows the money-motivation assumption creates compliance; Sinek shows the values-alignment assumption creates deep engagement. Together, they demonstrate that assumptions are not neutral but actively shape outcomes.

questions.q: Which of the following best captures the central throughline of Lecture 3?
options: Employees should prioritize salary above all else to ensure financial security
Meaning, engagement, and happiness are not soft extras but core drivers of performance and ethical responsibility
Businesses have no responsibility for employee well-being, only for profitability
The relationship between employers and employees is purely transactional
Employee happiness is irrelevant to business performance
questions.explain: The lecture introduction explicitly states: 'The central throughline is that meaning, engagement, and happiness are not soft extras — they are core drivers of performance and ethical responsibility.' This captures the overarching theme connecting all five sections and the employer-employee duties discussion.

questions.q: What is the relationship between flow state and the Good Life according to the lecture?
options: Flow state is unrelated to happiness or life satisfaction
Flow state is the mechanism through which the Good Life is achieved via absorption and engagement
The Good Life is only possible through the Pleasant Life; flow is irrelevant
The lecture does not discuss the connection between flow and the Good Life
Flow state prevents the achievement of the Good Life by consuming too much mental energy
questions.explain: The lecture table directly labels the Good Life as 'Engagement; absorption (投入) via flow state' and states: 'Work that provides these three conditions [clear goals, immediate feedback, challenge-skill match] enables the Good Life.' Flow is the defining mechanism of the Good Life in Seligman's framework.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is the core problem with Foxconn's initial responses to employee suicides?
options: The responses were too costly and reduced company profits
They addressed symptoms (pay, nets, pledges, support) rather than the root meaninglessness of the work itself
The responses were too generous and created dependency
The lecture does not evaluate the adequacy of Foxconn's responses
The responses improved morale but decreased productivity
questions.explain: The lecture notes state: 'Foxconn's responses are often mistaken for adequate solutions. The lecture treats them as evidence that addressing symptoms (financial pay, physical barriers) without addressing meaninglessness (無意義感) is ethically insufficient.' This is the core lesson: symptoms versus root causes.

questions.q: How does the concept of autonomy connect to Barry Schwartz's argument about worker motivation?
options: Autonomy is irrelevant to worker motivation; only money matters
Stripping autonomy from work reinforces the money-motivation assumption and undermines meaningful work
Autonomy should be unlimited and without any organizational structure
Autonomy is the only factor that matters in worker motivation
The lecture does not address the relationship between autonomy and motivation
questions.explain: The lecture states: 'When work is stripped of autonomy (自主性) and meaning, workers do in fact work only for money.' Autonomy is central to Schwartz's argument: loss of autonomy reinforces the money-motivation cycle and undermines intrinsic motivation and meaning.

questions.q: What does the lecture suggest about the potential tension between hiring for values alignment and avoiding manipulation?
options: There is no tension; manipulation is never a concern in hiring
The lecture frames this as a legitimate ethical concern: 'hiring for shared beliefs builds loyalty, but raises the question of manipulation versus authentic alignment'
Values alignment always requires manipulation to be effective
The lecture does not address this ethical tension
Manipulation is always justified if it produces loyal employees
questions.explain: The lecture notes explicitly state: 'The "brainwashing" concern (Simon Sinek quote): hiring for shared beliefs builds loyalty, but raises the question of manipulation (操縱) versus authentic alignment.' This acknowledges the ethical complexity of values-aligned hiring and does not dismiss the concern.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the psychological state of "flow" (心流) as described by Csikszentmihalyi?
options: A state of deep relaxation achieved through meditation and mindfulness practices
Complete absorption in a challenging activity where skills match the task demand
The feeling of contentment that comes from fulfilling basic physiological needs
A peak emotional state triggered by external rewards such as bonuses
The sense of pride derived from completing routine, easy tasks quickly
questions.explain: Flow occurs when a person is fully immersed in an activity that is challenging enough to match their skill level — neither too easy (boredom) nor too hard (anxiety). It is intrinsically motivated, not externally rewarded.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a supply chain (供應鏈)?
options: A network connecting only manufacturers and distributors
A network between a company and its suppliers to produce and distribute products, including activities, people, entities, and resources from raw materials to the final customer
The process of manufacturing a product in-house without external suppliers
A system that focuses only on transporting finished goods to retail stores
A contract between a company and a single primary supplier
questions.explain: A supply chain is a comprehensive network spanning the entire process from raw materials to final consumer delivery. The definition includes all key actors (suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, retailers, consumers) and is circular, not purely linear. Option A is too narrow (excludes retailers/consumers), C represents vertical integration, D is too limited (ignores upstream), and E confuses a single supplier contract with an entire network.

questions.q: In Zadek's five-stage framework, which stage best describes a company that says 'It's the stupid thing to do [not to act]'?
options: Defensive (防禦性)
Compliance (合規)
Managerial (管理性)
Strategic (策略性)
Civil (公民)
questions.explain: The Managerial stage is characterized by incorporating responsibility into core business processes with the attitude that inaction is foolish. Defensive denies responsibility ('not our job'), Compliance minimizes obligation ('just as much as we have to'), Strategic creates competitive edge, and Civil leads industry transformation.

questions.q: What was the primary financial consequence that forced Nike to shift from its Defensive stance on supplier responsibility?
options: Loss of a major retailer contract in Europe
A 69% drop in earnings in fiscal year 1998, worsened by Asian currency crisis and weak demand
A consumer boycott that reduced shoe sales by exactly 50%
Regulatory fines imposed by the US government for labor violations
A major product recall due to manufacturing defects
questions.explain: Nike's fiscal 1998 earnings declined 69% due to multiple factors (Asian currency crisis, oversupply, weak demand), not solely because of sweatshop allegations. However, this financial loss accomplished what hundreds of critical articles had not — it forced CEO Phil Knight to publicly admit wrongdoing. The financial impact, combined with campus backlash, drove the transition.

questions.q: According to Auret van Heerden's duty of care framework, which of the following is NOT a legitimate excuse for a corporation to avoid responsibility for supplier conduct?
options: The supplier is a private, independent contractor not owned by the company
The company does not directly manufacture products in-house
The company's supply chain is too complex to monitor
The company outsources production to reduce costs
The supplier's violations are discovered after the product is sold
questions.explain: The duty of care explicitly rejects the 'independent contractor' defense — outsourcing does not outsource ethical responsibility. The duty extends to ensuring that a product reaches the consumer without compromising safety or consumer conscience throughout the entire supply chain. The other options represent practical challenges but not legitimate ethical excuses under this framework.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a private regulation approach to supply chain responsibility?
options: Government-mandated compliance inspections
Supplier code of conduct (供應商行為準則)
International trade agreements
Vertical integration through company acquisition
Third-party certification by the International Labour Organization
questions.explain: A supplier code of conduct is a written set of minimum standards imposed by the buying company — a form of private regulation. Government inspections and trade agreements are public regulation. Vertical integration is a corporate structure choice, not a compliance mechanism. While third-party certification can support compliance, the code of conduct itself is the direct expression of private regulation.

questions.q: What do tantalum and tungsten have in common in the context of supply chain ethics?
options: They are both used exclusively in high-end luxury goods
They are both mined primarily in developed nations with strict labor standards
They are conflict minerals (衝突礦產) mined in conflict zones and sold to finance armed groups
They are both prohibited under the Dodd-Frank Act
They are both produced through sustainable fair-trade programs
questions.explain: Tantalum and tungsten are conflict minerals — extracted from conflict zones and sold to finance armed groups. The Dodd-Frank Act does not ban their sourcing but requires disclosure (Form SD).
