They are mined in resource-rich developing regions with weak governance, not primarily in developed nations with strict standards. They have multiple legitimate uses beyond luxury goods.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why incompleteness is a structural limitation of contracts?
options: Courts refuse to interpret ambiguous contract language
Parties lack the ability to foresee and specify every possible future contingency due to bounded rationality (有限理性)
Suppliers deliberately hide information from buyers
Contracts are too long and complex for anyone to read carefully
International trade agreements override domestic contracts
questions.explain: Incompleteness arises from bounded rationality — the cognitive limitation preventing parties from anticipating every future state and writing a comprehensive contract covering all contingencies. The other options involve different issues (interpretation, asymmetry, document length) or are outside the contract itself.

questions.q: Ex ante transaction costs occur at which phase of a business relationship?
options: During the contract execution phase
After the contract is signed and performance begins
Before the deal — at the search, negotiation, and contract-drafting stage
When disputes arise and must be resolved in court
Continuously throughout the relationship with no specific timing
questions.explain: Ex ante (事前) costs are incurred before the deal: searching for suppliers, negotiating terms, and drafting the contract. Ex post (事後) costs occur after — enforcing the contract and settling disputes. The exam trap is confusing ex ante with ex post.

questions.q: According to the lecture, trust (信任) reduces transaction costs primarily by decreasing which of the following?
options: The price of raw materials from suppliers
The time and money spent on monitoring, enforcement, and dispute resolution
The number of suppliers a company must hire
The legal fees associated with contract drafting
The geographical distance between buyer and supplier
questions.explain: When trust exists (predictable, dependable behavior), fewer resources are needed for monitoring, enforcement, and dispute resolution. Trust does not affect material prices, supplier count, drafting fees, or geography — it reduces the overhead costs of managing the relationship itself.

questions.q: A multi-tiered supply chain (like Nike's example) differs from a single-tier supply chain in that it includes:
options: Multiple retailers selling the same product under different brand names
Suppliers of raw materials (Tier 2) feeding into manufacturers (Tier 1), who supply the brand company
Multiple companies competing to supply the same final product
Different distribution channels but identical suppliers at each stage
Customers purchasing products directly from the manufacturer
questions.explain: Nike's multi-tiered structure has Tier 2 (raw materials: rubber, fabric) → Tier 1 (shoe manufacturing/assembly) → Nike's product development/marketing → retail channels. The tiers represent the depth of the supply chain, not competing suppliers or distribution variants at the same level.

questions.q: Why did Nike's initial defense based on lacking in-house manufacturing ultimately fail to protect the company from ethical responsibility claims?
options: The government banned outsourced manufacturing entirely
International labor courts ruled that all corporations must own their production facilities
The duty of care framework requires corporations to ensure ethical standards throughout the entire supply chain, not just in operations they directly own
Consumers refused to buy any products made by external manufacturers
The company could not afford to pay the legal fees for defending the case
questions.explain: The duty of care principle explicitly rejects the outsourcing defense — a corporation cannot escape responsibility by claiming its suppliers are independent. The duty extends to the entire supply chain regardless of ownership structure. No such government ban or court ruling exists; the ethical framework itself refutes this defense.

questions.q: When comparing Zadek's Defensive and Compliance stages, the key difference is that Compliance companies:
options: Admit wrongdoing and apologize to victims
Implement policies and manage risks while still viewing responsibility as an obligation to minimize
Integrate supplier responsibility into core business strategy for competitive advantage
Lead industry-wide transformation of supply chain standards
Completely eliminate all unethical practices in their supply chains
questions.explain: Compliance companies shift from denial to action ('we'll do just as much as we have to') — implementing policies to manage risks but still focused on value protection, not creation. Managerial stage integrates responsibility into processes; Strategic stage creates competitive advantage; Civil stage leads transformation. Compliance does not yet view ethics as a strategic opportunity.

questions.q: Supply chain auditing differs from supplier development in that auditing primarily:
options: Provides training and capability-building programs to suppliers
Verifies compliance with existing standards through internal, third-party, or crowdsourced methods
Requires the company to acquire the supplier as a subsidiary
Eliminates the need for contracts between buyer and supplier
Mandates that all suppliers join industry-wide associations
questions.explain: Auditing checks whether suppliers meet established standards; it is a verification mechanism. Supplier development goes beyond policing to include training, joint problem-solving, and root cause analysis. Auditing is backward-looking (compliance check); development is forward-looking (capability building).

questions.q: The Dodd-Frank Act's approach to conflict minerals can best be characterized as:
options: A complete ban on the purchase and use of conflict minerals
A mandatory disclosure requirement (Form SD) for US-listed companies using conflict minerals
A government subsidy to encourage conflict-free mining in developing nations
An international treaty that replaced all domestic supply chain regulations
A voluntary certification program with no legal enforcement mechanism
questions.explain: Dodd-Frank requires companies to file Form SD with the SEC disclosing their use of conflict minerals — a transparency measure, not a ban. The regulation does not subsidize alternatives, replace other laws, or rely on purely voluntary participation.

questions.q: According to the lecture, trustworthiness (可信賴性) requires which combination of attributes?
options: Only competence and reliability; honesty is assumed
Only reliability and honesty; competence is expected from professional suppliers
Competence, reliability, and honesty/integrity — all three must be demonstrated
Only honesty/integrity; competence and reliability follow naturally
Any two of the three; the third can be developed over time
questions.explain: Trustworthiness = Competence (ability to perform) + Reliability (consistent delivery) + Honesty/Integrity (ethical behavior). All three are necessary; lacking even one undermines the whole. The lecture emphasizes that trust must be earned through demonstrating all three components.

questions.q: When a supplier violates labor standards, when is exit the more rational choice than engagement?
options: When the supplier is the only qualified manufacturer in the industry
When the supplier is replaceable, the breach is severe and irreparable, or reputational risk outweighs switching costs
When the company has invested heavily in capability-building programs
When the supplier is a critical, hard-to-replace manufacturer like Foxconn
When the violation is systemic rather than willful misconduct
questions.explain: Exit is optimal when the supplier can be replaced, the breach is severe/irreparable, and reputational damage risk exceeds switching costs. Options C, D, and E all support engagement, not exit. Option D (irreplaceable supplier) specifically argues for engagement despite the violation.

questions.q: Non-verifiability as a contract limitation refers to which situation?
options: A supplier intentionally refuses to sign the written contract
Courts cannot order specific outcomes when disputes involve information asymmetry (信息不對稱) that the court cannot objectively verify
A contract is written in a language neither party fully understands
The contract does not specify a dispute resolution mechanism
One party has superior knowledge about product quality
questions.explain: Non-verifiability occurs when courts can only enforce outcomes that are objectively verifiable; many disputes involve asymmetric information that courts cannot resolve. This is a structural court limitation, not a contract-drafting issue or signing refusal.

questions.q: Why might vertical integration (垂直整合) through acquiring a supplier not be the optimal solution for enforcing supply chain ethics, despite guaranteeing direct control?
options: Acquisition is prohibited by antitrust laws in most countries
It introduces massive capital requirements, operational complexity, and loss of supply chain flexibility
Acquired suppliers immediately become more unethical under corporate ownership
Customers prefer to buy from companies that use independent suppliers
Vertical integration only works for companies with manufacturing facilities
questions.explain: Vertical integration would provide direct control and guarantee compliance but imposes heavy costs: massive capital investment, operational complexity, and reduced supply chain flexibility. These costs often outweigh the ethics-enforcement benefit. Apple's reliance on Foxconn demonstrates why engagement, not acquisition, is often more rational.

questions.q: The exam trap regarding Nike's 'independent contractor' defense is best understood as:
options: A legally valid shield that courts have since overturned
A real historical stance that the course frames as ethically inadequate under the duty of care, not a legitimate escape from responsibility
A strategy that worked in the 1990s but is now obsolete
Proof that outsourcing is always unethical
Evidence that the course supports Nike's position
questions.explain: Nike actually did use this defense, and it was a real historical position. However, the course frames it as a failure of duty of care, not a valid legal escape. The exam trap is failing to distinguish between what Nike claimed and what the ethical framework actually requires.

questions.q: How does the circular nature of supply chains (mentioned in the lecture) affect business decision-making compared to a linear model?
options: It eliminates the need for contracts between parties
It means customer needs/wants feedback flows back upstream, requiring companies to maintain relationships and responsiveness beyond simple transaction completion
It proves that all suppliers must be equally important to the buyer
It removes the possibility of exit if a supplier becomes unethical
It guarantees that ethical practices in one tier automatically spread to all other tiers
questions.explain: A circular supply chain means feedback flows back upstream — the buyer must remain engaged with suppliers beyond initial transaction. This reinforces the duty of care and the importance of long-term relationships and trust. It does not eliminate contracts, equalize supplier importance, prevent exit, or guarantee ethical propagation.

questions.q: Swire Properties' Supplier Code of Conduct addresses all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Child labour (童工) standards
Environmental impact assessment (環境影響)
Employee compensation and working hours
Climate change mitigation targets for suppliers
Forced labour (強迫勞動) prohibition
questions.explain: The lecture mentions Swire's code covers legal compliance, environment, child labor, forced labor, and compensation/working hours. Climate change mitigation targets are not explicitly listed as part of Swire's code in the lecture material. This tests careful attention to what was actually covered.

questions.q: Which combination of circumstances would make engagement (rather than exit) the optimal choice when a supplier commits an ethical violation?
options: The supplier is easily replaced, the breach is intentional, and reputational damage is minor
The supplier is critical and hard to replace, the issue is systemic rather than willful, and capability investment yields long-term compliance
The company has already exited three other suppliers that year
The supplier's violation was discovered after 10 years of successful partnership
The supplier's country of operation has recently changed government
questions.explain: Engagement is optimal when: (1) the supplier is critical/irreplaceable, (2) the issue is systemic (fixable through capability-building) rather than willful misconduct, and (3) investment in development will yield compliance. The Apple-Foxconn relationship exemplifies this logic.

questions.q: According to the lecture, contracts alone are insufficient to govern supply chain ethics primarily because:
options: Contracts are too expensive to write and enforce
Bounded rationality, information asymmetry, and self-interest create gaps that contracts cannot fully seal
Suppliers deliberately violate every contract clause
Courts refuse to enforce contracts involving ethical standards
International agreements prohibit detailed supply chain contracts
questions.explain: The three structural limitations (incompleteness from bounded rationality, non-verifiability from information asymmetry, and opportunism from self-interest) mean contracts cannot fully govern behavior. Trust must complement contracts to fill these gaps. The other options misstate the reason or are false.

questions.q: The Strategic stage of corporate responsibility evolution (according to Zadek) differs from the Managerial stage primarily in its underlying motivation:
options: Strategic companies deny responsibility; Managerial companies accept it
Strategic companies view responsibility as creating competitive value; Managerial companies incorporate it into processes but still emphasize value protection over creation
Strategic companies use auditing; Managerial companies use supplier development
Strategic companies only serve domestic markets; Managerial companies serve global markets
Strategic companies are larger; Managerial companies are smaller
questions.explain: Both Managerial and Strategic stages accept responsibility, but the mindset differs. Managerial integrates responsibility into core processes, still primarily protecting value. Strategic sees responsibility as a source of competitive edge and value creation. The table shows 'Value protection → creation' as the Managerial transition point and 'Value creation' for Strategic, indicating the shift in orientation.

questions.q: If a contract's non-verifiability problem prevents courts from enforcing a clause protecting workers' rights because wage theft is difficult to prove, what mechanism does the lecture suggest could reduce reliance on court enforcement?
options: Increasing the number of judges in labor courts
Building trust through demonstrated trustworthiness, which reduces the need for formal enforcement
Requiring suppliers to post collateral as a bond
Using the Dodd-Frank Act to prosecute wage theft
Hiring private investigators to monitor supplier compliance
questions.explain: When courts cannot verify or enforce specific wage protections, trust becomes critical — the company relies on the supplier's demonstrated honesty/integrity and reliability to ensure compliance without formal litigation. Trust reduces transaction costs by decreasing enforcement burden. The other options involve increased monitoring costs, not trust.

questions.q: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates the distinction between ex ante and ex post transaction costs?
options: Both costs apply equally to all suppliers regardless of relationship history
Ex ante: negotiating the hourly wage rate in a labor contract; Ex post: resolving a wage theft dispute after the contract period ends
Ex ante: auditing supplier compliance; Ex post: writing the supplier code of conduct
Ex ante: vertical integration; Ex post: outsourcing to suppliers
Both are incurred simultaneously at the moment the contract is signed
questions.explain: The wage negotiation occurs before the deal (ex ante); the dispute resolution after (ex post). This clearly shows the temporal distinction. The other pairings either reverse the categories or conflate different concepts (auditing vs. code-writing are not mirror ex ante/ex post costs).

questions.q: The lecture emphasizes that trust and contracts are complementary rather than substitutes in governing supply chains. This most directly implies that:
options: Companies should choose either trust or contracts, whichever is cheaper
High trust eliminates the need for any contractual documentation
Contracts establish the baseline standards, while trust bridges the gaps that contracts cannot fully cover due to bounded rationality and information asymmetry
Trust applies only to long-term suppliers; contracts apply only to new suppliers
The more detailed the contract, the less trust is needed in the relationship
questions.explain: The lecture states that trust reduces transaction costs but does not replace contracts — it complements contractual governance. Contracts set minimum standards; trust ensures predictable behavior beyond what contracts can specify due to their structural limitations (incompleteness, non-verifiability, and opportunism).

questions.q: A company discovers that its supplier is experiencing systemic labor management issues (e.g., inconsistent wage documentation, unclear shift scheduling) rather than intentional misconduct (e.g., deliberately withholding wages). According to the lecture's exit vs. engagement framework, which choice is more likely to be optimal?
options: Exit immediately to avoid reputational damage
Engage and invest in capability-building (training, root cause analysis, systems improvement) because systemic issues are fixable through development
Implement stricter auditing to catch violations
Reduce orders to minimize exposure while maintaining the relationship
File a formal complaint with the country's labor ministry
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that engagement is optimal 'when the issue is systemic rather than willful misconduct, and investment in capability building yields long-term compliance.' Systemic issues (poor processes, lack of training) are solvable; intentional misconduct is not. Supplier development (training, root cause analysis) directly addresses systemic problems.

questions.q: The duty of care's emphasis on protecting 'consumer conscience' as well as 'consumer safety' most directly reflects which underlying ethical principle?
options: Corporations must maximize shareholder profit above all other considerations
Consumers should not be forced to participate indirectly in unethical practices (e.g., funding labor abuse through their purchases) regardless of direct personal safety risk
All suppliers must meet identical standards regardless of local economic conditions
Corporations have no ethical responsibility beyond legal compliance
Vertical integration is the only way to ensure ethical supply chains
questions.explain: The lecture states that consumers must be able to consume 'without fear for their safety or having to sacrifice their conscience.' This extends duty of care beyond physical safety to include moral complicity. A consumer who unknowingly funds labor abuse may not face personal safety risk but faces a conscience harm — the duty addresses both. The other options contradict or are outside this framework.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why trust (信任) between a buyer and supplier can reduce transaction costs (交易成本)?
options: Trust allows buyers to avoid paying fair prices to suppliers
Trust reduces the need for detailed contracts and monitoring, lowering coordination costs
Trust eliminates the need for any written agreements in supply chains
Trust increases switching costs, making it harder to change suppliers
Trust replaces government regulation as the main enforcement mechanism
questions.explain: Trust lowers transaction costs by reducing the need for elaborate contracts and intensive monitoring. When parties trust each other, they spend less on negotiation, verification, and enforcement.

questions.q: What best defines a community in the context of corporate responsibility?
options: Only the geographical location where a company has offices
An organization's area of local influence plus any broader groups impacted by its actions
Groups that share financial interests with the company
Exclusively online followers of a company's social media
People who work for the company
questions.explain: A community encompasses both the local geographical area and any groups impacted by the firm's actions, reflecting the mutual dependence between business and society. Students often limit it to only geographical location or only customers.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four community types?
options: Site community
Fence-line community
Virtual communities
Upstream communities
Communities of interest
questions.explain: The four types are site, fence-line, virtual, and communities of interest. 'Upstream communities' is not a defined category. Students may confuse supply chain terms with community typology.

questions.q: A company gains local knowledge and innovative ideas from community engagement through which business benefit?
options: Competitiveness
Decision-making
Legitimacy
Brand awareness
Worker retention
questions.explain: Decision-making directly involves gaining community viewpoints and local knowledge. Competitiveness relates to operational ease; legitimacy to reducing conflict; brand awareness to visibility — but only decision-making captures the intellectual input benefit.

questions.q: According to the Cone/Echo Research cited in the lecture, what percentage of consumers consider CSR when making purchases?
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that CSR was a consideration for 82% of consumers according to Cone/Echo Research. This statistic underscores the market incentive for CSR engagement beyond purely ethical motives.

questions.q: How does corporate philanthropy differ from corporate social responsibility (CSR)?
options: They are synonymous terms used interchangeably
CSR is broader; philanthropy is a narrower subset of CSR
Philanthropy is broader; CSR is one type of philanthropy
CSR applies only to large corporations; philanthropy applies to all
Philanthropy focuses on shareholder returns; CSR focuses on society
questions.explain: CSR describes the overall organizational attitude toward society, while philanthropy is a narrower subset involving charitable donations and actions. Not all CSR is philanthropy, and not all philanthropic efforts constitute full CSR strategy.

questions.q: McKinsey's provision of free consulting to NGOs exemplifies which orientation dimension of philanthropic strategy?
options: Market orientation
Competence orientation
Community orientation
Ethical orientation
Shareholder orientation
questions.explain: Competence orientation aligns philanthropic initiatives with the company's core abilities and expertise. McKinsey provides consulting — its core competency — rather than responding to stakeholder expectations (market orientation).

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT listed as a priority focus area for corporate giving during 2015–2017?
options: Health/Wellbeing
STEM
Environment/Sustainability
Workforce/Employment
Education/Schools
questions.explain: The lecture lists tracked areas including Health/Wellbeing, STEM, Environment/Sustainability, Cancer, Military/Veterans, Safety, Diversity and Inclusion, and Workforce/Employment. Education/Schools is not explicitly mentioned in the 2015–2017 trends.

questions.q: What was the largest reported decrease in corporate priority focus areas between 2015 and 2017?
options: Disaster Relief (−8%)
Military/Veterans (−6%)
Education (−5%)
Heritage (−8%)
Safety (−4%)
questions.explain: Disaster Relief experienced the largest reported decrease at −8%. This likely reflects shifting priorities post-disaster relief cycles and a move toward long-term, systemic social investments.

questions.q: Which Corporate Responsibility Action Type is represented by Mars raising its CSR bar in supply chain practices?
options: Philanthropy Type
Integration Type
Innovation Type
Transformation Type
Charitable Type
questions.explain: Integration Type focuses on conducting existing business operations more responsibly. Mars's supply chain improvement is an integration of CSR into core operations, not a new business model (Innovation) or charitable giving (Philanthropy).

questions.q: What is the primary innovation in Unilever's Project Shakti?
options: Providing free hygiene products to Indian villages
Opening retail stores in rural areas
Creating a new business model combining microfinance with product sales and training
Establishing a foundation to fund women's education
Developing cheaper hygiene products for emerging markets
questions.explain: Project Shakti combines microfinance loans, training, and product sales to empower rural women while creating a profitable distribution channel. This simultaneous addressing of social needs and revenue generation exemplifies the Innovation Type.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of Nan Fung's Philanthropy Type CSR action?
options: D.H. Chen Foundation
Employee volunteering for WWF
Lifeline Express flag sales
ISO 14001:2004 Environmental Management System
Hang Seng environmental awards
questions.explain: ISO 14001:2004 is an Integration Type action — improving existing operations. The Foundation, volunteering, and flag sales are all Philanthropy Type examples. Students often conflate CSR types.

questions.q: In which decade did CSR evolve from a defensive, compliance-only approach to philanthropic corporate citizenship?
questions.explain: The 1970s were defensive (legal requirements only), and the 1980s introduced the philanthropic (corporate citizenship) phase. This marks the shift from purely reactive compliance to proactive giving.

questions.q: What term describes the CSR evolution phase of the 1990s?
options: Strategic value
Cause-related marketing
Transformative management
Defensive compliance
Reputation management
questions.explain: The 1990s introduced cause-related marketing as a key CSR phase, where companies leveraged marketing alongside charitable initiatives. The 2000s advanced to strategic value; 2012 brought transformative management.

questions.q: According to Porter & Kramer, Creating Shared Value (CSV) can best be distinguished from philanthropy by which characteristic?
options: Philanthropy involves cash donations; CSV does not
CSV creates new value rather than redistributing existing value
Philanthropy targets communities; CSV targets corporations
CSV requires government involvement; philanthropy does not
Philanthropy is tax-deductible; CSV is not
questions.explain: CSV creates new value by integrating social improvement into competitive strategy, whereas philanthropy redistributes value already created. CSV is planned and strategic; philanthropy is often one-time giving.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of Creating Shared Value (CSV)?
options: Enhancing company competitiveness
Advancing social and environmental conditions
Sharing value already created
Being planned and strategic
Treating societal problems as internal costs
questions.explain: CSV explicitly is NOT sharing value already created — that is philanthropy. CSV creates new value. The exam trap here is confusing CSV with charitable redistribution of pre-existing returns.

questions.q: According to the CSV framework, where does shared value exist?
options: At the intersection of social needs and business opportunities
At the intersection of social needs, business opportunities, and corporate assets
Purely in the social sector
Purely in the business sector
In shareholder returns only
questions.explain: The lecture's Venn diagram and text explicitly state that CSV operates at the intersection of social needs, business opportunities, AND corporate assets — a three-way intersection, not just two dimensions.

questions.q: What type of real estate investment trust is Link REIT?
options: A non-profit organization
Hong Kong's largest REIT operating retail markets and car parks
A government agency
A private equity firm
A charitable foundation
questions.explain: Link REIT (領展房產基金) is explicitly described as Hong Kong's largest real estate investment trust, operating retail markets and car parks inherited from public housing estates.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Link REIT's renovations caused social conflict?
options: Construction delays disrupted shopping
Rent increases pushed out small tenants and raised the cost of living for vulnerable communities
Parking fees became too expensive
Environmental damage from construction
Employee layoffs from renovation
questions.explain: Renovations necessitated rent increases that hurt small tenants (fruits and vegetables vendors) and vulnerable communities. This gentrification effect is the core tension between profit and social responsibility.

questions.q: How did Hong Kong's chief executive characterize Link REIT's role in the city?
options: A major employer
One of the 'big three mountains' — a major burden on citizens
A model of corporate governance
A provider of affordable housing
A symbol of Hong Kong progress
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that the chief executive labeled Link REIT's role as one of Hong Kong's 'big three mountains' (三座大山) — a major societal burden, reflecting public vilification.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a Link REIT stakeholder?
options: Shareholders like BlackRock
Small fruit and vegetable vendors
Municipal government
General public and NGOs
International labor unions
questions.explain: The lecture lists shareholders, unit holders, tenants, customers, municipal government, general public, NGOs, and media. International labor unions are not mentioned as a stakeholder group.

questions.q: Why does Link REIT's rent increase strategy directly harm the firm's relationship with which stakeholder group?
options: Shareholders
Institutional investors
Small tenants and low-income customers
Government regulators
Media organizations
questions.explain: Renovation and rent increases directly harm small tenants (who are pushed out) and low-income customers (who face higher prices). This creates the gentrification conflict central to the case.

questions.q: According to the lecture, how does Link REIT's renovations benefit one group while harming another?
options: Benefits tenants; harms shareholders
Benefits customers; harms government
Benefits institutional investors and unit holders; harms poor tenants and low-income customers
Benefits government; harms the public
Benefits employees; harms management
questions.explain: Renovations increase returns for shareholders and unit holders but raise rents, directly harming small tenants and low-income customers. This is a classic stakeholder conflict between profit and social welfare.

questions.q: What is the business logic (not ethical logic) for Link REIT to adopt social responsibility practices?
options: It is legally required by government
Public vilification damages image; government pressure damages relations; a prosperous, inclusive community increases long-term returns
Shareholder activism demands it
International law mandates it
Competitors are doing it
questions.explain: The lecture emphasizes that Link REIT's rationale for social responsibility is business-driven: improved image, better government relations, and higher long-term revenue from a prosperous community — not purely ethical obligation.

questions.q: How can an inclusive community approach benefit Link REIT's financial returns according to the lecture?
options: It reduces property taxes
A prosperous, inclusive community attracts higher-income residents and educated workers, increasing tenant income and Link REIT revenue
It eliminates regulatory compliance costs
It increases shareholder activism
It reduces operational complexity
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that a prosperous community attracts higher-income and educated residents, boosting tenant income and Link REIT revenue. Inclusive growth and high returns are not mutually exclusive.

questions.q: What two components are recommended for resolving Link REIT's conflicting stakeholder interests?
options: Increase rents and improve marketing
Balance social and economic interests; undertake shared value creation
Relocate operations and sell assets
Reduce employee compensation and increase charity
Divest from the market
questions.explain: The resolution involves balancing social interests with economic interests to gain operational legitimacy, and undertaking CSV to define the intersection of social needs, business opportunities, and corporate assets.

questions.q: What concept does the lecture suggest Link REIT should adopt to address gentrification concerns while maintaining profitability?
options: Pure philanthropy
Creating Shared Value
Government subsidies
Market monopoly
Price controls
questions.explain: Creating Shared Value is explicitly presented as the framework for Link REIT to resolve conflicting interests by integrating social improvement into competitive strategy rather than treating gentrification as an external cost.

questions.q: Which organizational element should Link REIT's urban redevelopment set to encourage rejuvenation?
options: Shareholder voting rights
Predefined community standards
Quarterly financial targets
Executive compensation packages
Stock price thresholds
questions.explain: The lecture recommends setting predefined community standards in urban redevelopment and incorporating local stakeholders into the redevelopment process to balance growth with community welfare.

questions.q: What fundamental mindset shift does CSV require from corporations according to the lecture?
options: Prioritize shareholders over all stakeholders
Treat societal problems as internal costs rather than externalities
Eliminate all government regulation
Focus exclusively on profit maximization
Abandon market competition
questions.explain: The CSV mindset requires discarding the concept of 'externality' and treating societal problems as internal costs to the company. This reframes social responsibility from external compliance to core strategy.

questions.q: What distinguishes "strategic philanthropy" (策略性慈善) from traditional corporate donations?
options: Strategic philanthropy donates larger sums of money to charities
Strategic philanthropy aligns giving with the company's core business to create mutual benefit
Strategic philanthropy focuses exclusively on environmental causes
Strategic philanthropy requires government approval before donations are made
Strategic philanthropy only supports international NGOs rather than local communities
questions.explain: Strategic philanthropy links charitable activities to the company's core business strengths and strategy, creating value for both the community and the firm — unlike purely reactive or disconnected donations.

questions.q: In the Link REIT case, which stakeholder group most directly opposed the company's market-rate rental increases?
options: Institutional investors seeking higher dividends
Government housing authorities
Small retailers and wet market vendors serving low-income residents
International NGOs advocating for sustainable development
Competing real estate investment trusts
questions.explain: Small retailers and wet market vendors in public housing estates were most directly affected by Link REIT's rent increases after privatisation, as their customer base consisted of low-income residents who could not absorb higher prices.

lectures.title: Lecture 7: Business and the Natural Environment

questions.q: According to the stakeholder power-interest matrix discussed in the lecture, why is the natural environment classified as problematic to place in a single quadrant?
options: It has low power over businesses and minimal interest in their activities
It has immense power to influence businesses but cannot express interest in the human sense
It is a conventional stakeholder with legal standing and expressed preferences
It belongs in the Low Power, High Interest quadrant by definition
It has no impact on supply chains or business operations
questions.explain: The lecture states that nature has immense power (it can collapse supply chains and destroy assets) yet cannot express 'interest' in the human sense, making it difficult to place in a single quadrant. The incorrect answers misrepresent nature's power or assume false stakeholder characteristics.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the 'Nature Is Speaking' campaign by Conservation International?
options: It presents nature as an autonomous actor that does not need humans, while humans need nature
It positions humans and nature as mutual stakeholders with equal power
It frames nature as dependent on human protection and care
It argues that nature should be given legal rights and corporate representation
It demonstrates that environmental regulations effectively control business behavior
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly describes the campaign (with nature voiced by Julia Roberts) as framing nature as not needing humans — the relationship is reversed. The other options mischaracterize the campaign's core message about dependency.

questions.q: The five categories of global environmental challenges identified in the lecture include climate change, ozone depletion, resource scarcity, biodiversity decline, and which of the following?
options: Threats to marine ecosystems
Urban sprawl and deforestation
Agricultural overproduction
Industrial waste disposal
Renewable energy transition costs
questions.explain: The lecture lists threats to marine ecosystems (ocean degradation, coral reefs, fisheries) as the fifth category. The other options are related to environmental issues but are not the five specific categories named.

questions.q: Greenhouse gases mentioned in the lecture as drivers of climate change include carbon dioxide, methane, and which of the following?
options: Sulphur dioxide
Nitrous oxide
Nitrogen dioxide
Ozone molecules
Carbon monoxide
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly names carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide as greenhouse gases driving climate change. The other gases are environmental pollutants but are not identified as the three key greenhouse gases in this context.

questions.q: How does the lecture define greenwashing?
options: The use of recycled materials in product manufacturing
An unsubstantiated or misleading claim about environmental benefits that makes a company appear greener than it truly is
The government regulation of environmental practices in industry
The process of converting green waste into usable compost
Any marketing campaign that features the color green or natural imagery
questions.explain: This is the direct definition provided in the lecture. Greenwashing specifically harms both business credibility and actual environmental outcomes through false or exaggerated claims. The other options describe unrelated environmental practices or misdefine the term.

questions.q: Which of the Seven Sins of Greenwashing refers to a technically true claim that is not a meaningful differentiator?
options: Fibbing
Vagueness
Irrelevance
No Proof
Hidden Trade-Off
questions.explain: The lecture identifies Irrelevance (Sin #4) as claims that are technically true but unremarkable, such as 'CFC-Free' when CFCs are already banned by law. This differs from Vagueness, which uses broad, poorly defined terms. Students often confuse these two sins.

questions.q: The 'Lesser of Two Evils' sin of greenwashing is exemplified by which scenario?
options: A product claiming to be energy-efficient without supporting data
An organic cigarette marketed as greener than conventional cigarettes
A recycled-content product with high manufacturing energy use
Using fake third-party certification labels on packaging
A vague term like 'all-natural' that includes harmful naturally occurring ingredients
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly provides the organic cigarette example to illustrate Sin #5: being the greenest option in a category that is inherently unfriendly. Options with no proof or vague claims represent other sins, not this one.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) in the context of avoiding greenwashing?
options: To evaluate all inputs and outputs across a product's full life cycle, ensuring no narrow claims are made
To certify that products meet government environmental standards
To increase the price of sustainable products in the market
To replace traditional marketing with environmental messaging
To eliminate all non-recyclable materials from manufacturing
questions.explain: The lecture describes LCA as a systems thinking tool that evaluates the full life cycle from raw material acquisition through disposal. This comprehensive approach prevents companies from hiding negative impacts in overlooked stages. It is a recommended framework based on ISO 14040:2006.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what key insight does the electric hand dryer versus paper towel example illustrate about Life Cycle Assessment?
options: Full-cycle analysis can reveal non-obvious environmental winners that simple comparisons miss
Electric hand dryers are always more environmentally friendly
Paper towels have zero environmental impact when recycled
Manufacturing processes are the only stage that matters in LCA
Environmental impact is determined solely by end-of-life disposal
questions.explain: The lecture uses this comparative LCA to show that comprehensive analysis across all stages (materials, manufacturing, transportation, use, end-of-life) can reveal counterintuitive results. This prevents greenwashing by uncovering hidden impacts.

questions.q: What is the main environmental benefit highlighted in the cold-water detergent innovation example?
options: Significant energy savings and CO₂ emissions reduction if widely adopted
Reduced cost for detergent manufacturers
Elimination of harmful chemical residues in wastewater
Improved water quality in treated effluent
Enhanced fabric softness and durability
questions.explain: The lecture specifies that if all U.S. households switched to cold water, the energy saved would be equivalent to 4 years of Hoover Dam output, with CO₂ reduction up to 11 million metric tonnes per year. This dramatic environmental upside is offset by market resistance.

questions.q: According to the lecture, why did cold-water detergent fail commercially despite its substantial environmental and cost benefits?
options: Consumers were unaware of the environmental benefits
Consumer beliefs about hot water and marketing mismatch: environmental messaging is less effective than performance and price messaging
The product was more expensive than hot-water alternatives
Regulatory barriers prevented its widespread distribution
Technical limitations prevented it from effectively removing stains
questions.explain: The lecture identifies two key reasons: (1) consumer belief (passed-down conviction that hot water works best); (2) marketing mismatch (environmental benefits are weak persuaders; performance and price messaging are stronger). This illustrates the attitude-behavior gap.

questions.q: The attitude-behavior gap refers to the disconnect between:
options: Environmental beliefs and sustainable purchasing behavior
Government regulations and consumer compliance
Corporate social responsibility and actual environmental impact
Marketing claims and product quality
Recycling awareness and waste management practices
questions.explain: The lecture defines the attitude-behavior gap as the phenomenon where consumers hold pro-environmental attitudes (e.g., believing cold-water detergent is superior) yet fail to purchase or use sustainable products. Cold-water detergent exemplifies this gap.

questions.q: Status quo bias, as explained in the lecture, is best understood as which of the following?
options: A framing effect where any deviation from the default is perceived as a loss, even if the alternative is objectively superior
The natural human tendency to be lazy and resist any change
A lack of information preventing consumers from making better choices
The government's failure to incentivize sustainable behavior
Corporate resistance to improving environmental practices
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that status quo bias is NOT laziness or ignorance; it is a loss-aversion effect where people use the current baseline as a reference point. This is a critical exam trap because students often mischaracterize it as mere inertia.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what does 'discounting the distant future' mean in the context of environmental inaction?
options: People perceive environmental problems as psychologically distant in time and space, reducing their urgency and motivation
Environmental problems are financially expensive to solve
Future generations will develop better technologies than we can today
International climate agreements are not legally binding
Individuals should not invest in future sustainability efforts
questions.explain: The lecture identifies this as one of four mental barriers: people feel environmental problems are distant in time and space, making them less psychologically urgent. This reduces motivation to act despite understanding the problem.

questions.q: In the public goods dilemma (free-rider problem) described in the lecture, what does the statement 'The greatest threat to our planet is the belief that someone else will save it' imply?
options: Each individual waits for others to act, resulting in collective inaction
Individual action is insignificant and only collective policy matters
Governments must impose strict environmental regulations on all businesses
Environmental technology companies are responsible for solving climate change
Consumers should boycott environmentally harmful products
questions.explain: The lecture uses this quote to illustrate the public goods dilemma: when each person believes 'someone else will save the planet,' no one takes action, leading to collective failure. It demonstrates how individual responsibility diffuses in groups.

questions.q: What psychological finding does the research by Brough and Wilkie (2017) reveal about male consumers and green behavior?
options: Men resist green behavior as 'unmanly,' but masculine branding can eliminate this gender gap
Men are naturally more inclined to support environmental causes than women
Environmental messaging is equally persuasive to men and women in all contexts
Gender stereotypes have no influence on purchasing decisions
Women are less likely to purchase green products than men
questions.explain: The lecture describes the empirical finding: conventional green branding suppressed male donations relative to women; masculine green branding eliminated the gap. This shows the green-feminine stereotype is a real barrier that can be overcome with appropriate framing.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which of the following is NOT one of the four mental barriers to sustainable behavior?
options: Lack of scientific evidence for climate change
Status quo bias
Discounting the distant future
Public goods dilemma
Green-feminine stereotype
questions.explain: The lecture identifies exactly four barriers: status quo bias, discounting the distant future, public goods dilemma, and green-feminine stereotype. Lack of scientific evidence is not mentioned; the lecture assumes environmental problems are real and accepted.

questions.q: How does the HKUST water fountain example illustrate the behavioral change mechanism of progress monitoring?
options: It displays the number of plastic bottles saved, giving users real-time feedback on their collective impact
It provides immediate financial rewards to users who save water
It restricts water access to encourage conservation
It requires users to sign sustainability pledges
It replaces water fountains with alternative beverage systems
questions.explain: The lecture uses this campus example to show how progress monitoring (visible, real-time feedback on plastic bottles saved) makes behavior change tangible and reinforces continued action. This addresses the gap between future environmental benefits and present behavior.

questions.q: What are the two mechanisms the lecture proposes for motivating behavioral change?
options: Immediate reward and progress monitoring
Government regulation and financial penalties
Celebrity endorsements and social media campaigns
Price increases on unsustainable products
Corporate sustainability reporting and transparency
questions.explain: The lecture identifies immediate reward (short-term incentives bridging future benefits to present behavior) and progress monitoring (visible feedback reinforcing action) as evidence-based mechanisms. The HKUST water fountain example demonstrates progress monitoring.

questions.q: According to the lecture, how can companies like Starbucks leverage understanding of mental barriers to increase customer engagement in green efforts?
options: By designing interventions around psychological biases rather than simply informing consumers
By increasing prices on non-sustainable products
By publishing detailed environmental impact reports
By requiring customers to complete environmental education courses
By eliminating single-use products entirely without alternatives
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly suggests that companies should design around biases (e.g., overcoming status quo bias with convenient reusable options, addressing green-feminine stereotype with inclusive framing) rather than relying on information alone.

questions.q: Which greenwashing sin is most directly addressed by the use of Life Cycle Assessment tools like SimaPro?
options: Hidden Trade-Off — claiming eco-friendliness on narrow attributes while ignoring broader impacts
Fibbing — fabricating false certifications
No Proof — making claims without accessible evidence
Worshipping False Labels — creating fake third-party endorsements
Vagueness — using undefined terms like 'all-natural'
questions.explain: LCA's comprehensive evaluation of all inputs, outputs, and life cycle stages directly counters Hidden Trade-Off by preventing companies from highlighting one narrow benefit while concealing negative impacts elsewhere. This is the core purpose of systems thinking in avoiding greenwashing.

questions.q: The lecture mentions Deloitte sustainability services, Sustainable Minds, and SimaPro as examples of what?
options: Tools used in practice to conduct Life Cycle Assessment
Government agencies regulating environmental practices
Certification programs that guarantee greenwashing prevention
Corporate sustainability reporting standards
Non-profit organizations advocating for environmental protection
questions.explain: The lecture lists these as practical tools used to implement LCA frameworks based on ISO 14040:2006. They help companies systematically evaluate environmental impacts across product life cycles, not as certifications but as analytical tools.

questions.q: What insight does the lecture provide about the relationship between consumer knowledge and sustainable behavior?
options: Knowledge alone is insufficient; psychological barriers, beliefs, and effective messaging are equally critical
Providing more environmental information automatically increases sustainable purchases
Consumers who understand climate science are more likely to act sustainably
Sustainable behavior is determined primarily by educational level
Environmental awareness campaigns are the most cost-effective way to change behavior
questions.explain: The cold-water detergent case and the mental barriers section demonstrate that knowledge does not directly translate to action. Consumer beliefs (hot water works best), psychological barriers (status quo bias), and marketing messaging (performance over environment) often override factual information.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes why closed-loop recycling and remanufacturing are important elements of Life Cycle Assessment?
options: They feed recycled materials back into earlier production stages, reducing overall environmental impact across cycles
They eliminate the need for raw material extraction entirely
They guarantee that all products are 100% environmentally sustainable
They are the only stage of LCA that requires government oversight
They replace the need for Life Cycle Assessment entirely
questions.explain: The lecture explains that closed-loop recycling and remanufacturing allow materials to re-enter earlier stages of production, reducing the demand for new raw material extraction. This is a key strategy for minimizing environmental impact across the full product life cycle.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is the primary flaw in focusing solely on a product's end-of-life stage when assessing environmental impact?
options: It overlooks significant impacts from raw material extraction, manufacturing, transportation, and use stages that occur earlier in the product's life cycle
Consumers do not care about disposal practices
End-of-life recycling has no environmental benefit
The government already regulates disposal practices adequately
Recycling programs are too expensive to implement
questions.explain: The exam trap in the lecture emphasizes that LCA spans the FULL product life cycle, not just end-of-life. Students often reduce LCA to recycling or disposal only, missing impacts from extraction, processing, manufacturing, transportation, and use — often the dominant stages.

questions.q: How does the lecture's discussion of the natural environment as a stakeholder challenge traditional stakeholder theory?
options: It demonstrates that conventional categories (power and interest) are insufficient for non-human actors that have power without articulated preferences
It argues that nature has no power over businesses
It proves that environmental regulations are unnecessary
It suggests that nature should be given voting rights in corporate governance
It reveals that stakeholder analysis is irrelevant to modern businesses
questions.explain: The lecture identifies a fundamental problem: nature has enormous power (supply chain disruption, asset destruction) yet cannot express interest in the human sense, making it difficult to fit into the standard High Power/High Interest framework. This reveals a limitation of traditional stakeholder theory.

questions.q: Which combination of factors best explains the market failure of cold-water detergent despite its superior energy profile?
options: Deep consumer beliefs about washing effectiveness, combined with ineffective environmental messaging
Environmental regulations banned hot water and consumer distrust of new products
Technical product failure combined with lack of government subsidies
Manufacturer price-fixing and anti-competitive practices
Scientific uncertainty about the environmental benefits of cold water
questions.explain: The lecture identifies two interacting factors: (1) psychological—consumers believe hot water works better, a belief passed down generationally; (2) marketing—environmental benefits are weak persuaders compared to performance/price messaging. This is a case study in the attitude-behavior gap.

questions.q: What does the research on masculine green branding suggest about how to overcome the green-feminine stereotype?
options: Reframing sustainability initiatives with identity cues that align with masculine values can neutralize gender barriers and increase male participation
The stereotype is immutable and cannot be influenced by marketing
Women should be the exclusive target for green products
Environmental causes should avoid any association with gender
Male consumers will never support green behavior regardless of marketing strategy
questions.explain: The Brough & Wilkie (2017) study shows that masculine branding (e.g., framing green behavior as strong, practical, powerful) eliminated the gender gap in donation likelihood. This demonstrates that stereotypes are not fixed but can be overcome through appropriate framing.

questions.q: According to the lecture, immediate reward mechanisms for behavioral change are designed to address which psychological challenge?
options: The gap between future environmental benefits and present behavior motivations
The inability of consumers to understand environmental science
Government failure to regulate corporate environmental practices
The high cost of sustainable products
Consumer preference for non-renewable resources
questions.explain: The lecture explains that immediate rewards bridge the temporal gap: environmental benefits (e.g., energy savings from cold water) are distant and abstract, while present discomfort (hot-water habit) is concrete. Immediate incentives make the change feel rewarding now.

questions.q: In the context of the lecture, what distinguishes 'No Proof' from 'Vagueness' as sins of greenwashing?
options: 'No Proof' is a claim without accessible evidence or supporting data; 'Vagueness' uses broad, poorly defined terms that cannot be properly understood
'No Proof' involves unclear terminology; 'Vagueness' involves missing evidence
Both terms mean the same thing and are interchangeable
'Vagueness' applies only to advertising; 'No Proof' applies only to labels
'No Proof' is more common than 'Vagueness' in modern greenwashing
questions.explain: The lecture distinguishes these clearly: 'No Proof' is the absence of supporting evidence (e.g., energy-efficient bulb with no data); 'Vagueness' is the use of undefined terms (e.g., 'all-natural' that includes harmful ingredients). The exam trap is confusing these two distinct sins.

lectures.title: Lecture 8: Strategy and Innovation for Sustainability

questions.q: Which of the following best defines a sustainable society?
options: A society that completely eliminates industrial pollution
A society that meets present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own needs
A society that prioritizes economic growth above environmental concerns
A society with zero carbon emissions
A society that focuses exclusively on renewable energy adoption
questions.explain: The lecture defines sustainable society as meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own needs. This is the foundational definition that underpins all strategic approaches to sustainability. The other options are either too narrow (focusing only on pollution or carbon) or contradictory (prioritizing growth alone).

questions.q: What are the three pillars of the triple bottom line for a sustainable business?
options: Energy, Water, Waste
People, Planet, Profit
Innovation, Efficiency, Compliance
Supply Chain, Operations, Distribution
Community, Environment, Governance
questions.explain: The triple bottom line consists of People, Planet, and Profit. A sustainable business thrives in perpetuity by balancing all three. While other frameworks exist (ESG, lifecycle categories), the triple bottom line is the specific framework cited in this lecture for defining sustainable business.

questions.q: Which statement about sustainability represents the strongest counterargument presented in the lecture?
options: Most species become extinct, so sustainability is unachievable
Consumption behavior alone determines sustainability outcomes
New technology is always the solution to sustainability challenges
Sustainability is primarily a cost burden on business
Regulatory compliance ensures business sustainability
questions.explain: The lecture presents three debate positions, one of which is the existential argument that 'most species ultimately become extinct, so sustainability is a false proposition.' This challenges whether long-run sustainability is even possible. The other statements are either demand-side blame or technology-focused views, which are less philosophically fundamental.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which of the following is a reason why some argue new technology is essential for sustainability?
options: Because consumer preferences cannot change without incentives
Because it is virtually impossible to achieve sustainability without technological innovation
Because regulatory frameworks are insufficient on their own
Because circular economy models cannot function at scale
Because business models alone cannot address sustainability
questions.explain: The lecture mentions 'Without new technology, it's virtually impossible to achieve sustainability' as one of the three common debate positions addressed. This reflects a view that technological advancement is a prerequisite for solving sustainability challenges. While other factors matter, technology is positioned as a critical enabler.

questions.q: On the sustainability strategy matrix, which strategy is positioned in the Internal/Present quadrant?
options: Product Stewardship
Clean Technology
Sustainability Vision
Eco-efficiency
Stakeholder Integration
questions.explain: Eco-efficiency is the Internal/Present strategy, focused on minimizing waste and emissions from operations. Product Stewardship is External/Present, Clean Technology is Internal/Future, and Sustainability Vision is External/Future. Students frequently confuse eco-efficiency with product stewardship—this is an exam trap highlighted in the notes.

questions.q: Which sustainability strategy is characterized by developing new processes and materials for long-term competitive advantage?
options: Eco-efficiency
Product Stewardship
Clean Technology
Sustainability Vision
Resource Optimization
questions.explain: Clean Technology (Internal/Future) requires R&D investment in entirely new processes and materials to build sustainable competencies for the future. This distinguishes it from eco-efficiency (which optimizes existing operations) and product stewardship (which manages current lifecycle). Clean Technology is forward-looking and requires significant investment.

questions.q: M&S 'Plan A' slogan 'Because there is no Plan B' exemplifies which sustainability strategy?
options: Eco-efficiency
Product Stewardship
Clean Technology
Sustainability Vision
Circular Supply Chain
questions.explain: This slogan illustrates Sustainability Vision (External/Future), the most ambitious strategy that reframes the company's purpose around solving large societal challenges. The phrase suggests a company-wide commitment to sustainability as the only viable path forward, not a marginal operational improvement. This is the hallmark of Sustainability Vision positioning.

questions.q: Product Stewardship differs from Eco-efficiency primarily in which dimension?
options: It targets external stakeholders rather than internal operations
It requires more capital investment
It focuses on the future rather than the present
It eliminates the need for regulatory compliance
It prioritizes profit over environmental impact
questions.explain: Product Stewardship (External/Present) moves beyond internal operations to manage the full product lifecycle with stakeholder input, whereas Eco-efficiency (Internal/Present) minimizes waste and emissions from operations alone. The key distinction is scope: internal operations versus external stakeholder engagement and lifecycle management.

questions.q: How does the experience economy differ from a commodity-based economy in terms of sustainability?
options: It requires more energy to deliver
It generates higher customer satisfaction and less physical waste
It eliminates the need for product innovation
It increases consumer spending without improving wellbeing
It shifts responsibility entirely to the supply chain
questions.explain: The lecture notes that in the experience economy (commodity → good → service → experience), selling experiences commands higher value and generates less physical waste. Additionally, research shows experiential purchases retain higher satisfaction over time (5.42 vs 4.67 on a 1–7 scale at 4 weeks post-consumption). This reduces both material waste and improves long-term satisfaction.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes business model innovation in the context of sustainability?
options: Improving product efficiency through incremental design changes
Adjusting the business model at a fundamental level, such as new revenue streams or distribution channels
Reducing operational costs through workforce optimization
Adopting new certifications and compliance standards
Expanding into new geographic markets with existing products
questions.explain: Business model innovation is defined as adjusting the model at a fundamental level—for example, new revenue streams or distribution channels. This is distinct from incremental product improvements; it represents structural change in how the organization delivers value. Examples include moving to circular economy models or experience-based revenue.

questions.q: Which term best describes a regenerative system that minimizes resource input, waste, emissions, and energy leakage?
options: Linear supply chain
Circular economy
Lean manufacturing
Zero-waste production
Sustainable procurement
questions.explain: The circular economy is explicitly defined in the lecture as 'a regenerative system in which resource input and waste, emission, and energy leakage are minimized by slowing, closing, and narrowing material and energy loops.' This definition captures the essence of circular thinking: regeneration rather than depletion.

questions.q: The Adidas x Parley shoes made from ocean plastic exemplify which circular business model?
options: Circular Supplies
Product Life Extension
Sharing Platforms
Resource Recovery
Product as a Service
questions.explain: Adidas x Parley shoes are an example of Resource Recovery, which recovers useful resources from disposed products or by-products. Ocean plastic pollution is converted into a sellable product; each pair prevents approximately 11 plastic bottles from entering oceans. This transforms a waste stream into a valuable input.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes Product as a Service from a Sharing Platform?
options: Product as a Service is less profitable for the provider
The provider retains ownership in Product as a Service; users share access in Sharing Platforms
Sharing Platforms require digital technology; Product as a Service does not
Product as a Service creates lower environmental impact
Sharing Platforms are only viable in urban markets
questions.explain: In Product as a Service (e.g., Philips 'light as a service'), the provider retains ownership and internalizes productivity benefits. In Sharing Platforms (e.g., Airbnb, Uber), users share access among themselves. The critical distinguishing feature is ownership and incentive alignment: PaaS providers are incentivized to make products durable and efficient; Sharing Platforms enable peer-to-peer access without provider ownership.

questions.q: How does Philips' 'light as a service' arrangement benefit all three stakeholders (airport, Philips, environment)?
options: The airport gains lower energy bills; Philips gains market dominance; the environment gains waste reduction
The airport avoids upfront investment and maintenance; Philips gains incentive to produce efficient lights and reuse materials; the environment gains material recycling and reuse
The airport gains ownership of Philips technology; Philips gains guaranteed revenue; the environment gains pollution reduction
All stakeholders benefit equally from a reduced carbon footprint
The airport transfers all responsibility to Philips for environmental compliance
questions.explain: The lecture emphasizes a 'win-win-win': the airport gains no upfront investment burden and no maintenance hassle; Philips gains an incentive to manufacture the most energy-efficient lights and reuse recycled materials (since Philips pays the electricity bills); the environment gains because materials are effectively recycled and reused. This alignment of incentives is the power of the Product as a Service model.

questions.q: Patagonia's 'Worn Wear' program exemplifies which circular business model?
options: Circular Supplies
Resource Recovery
Product Life Extension
Sharing Platforms
Product as a Service
questions.explain: Patagonia's Worn Wear program (free repair, 1% of sales donated, swap events, product recycling) extends the working lifecycle of products through repair, upgrading, and reselling. This is the definition of Product Life Extension. The lecture notes that fashion is the second most polluting industry, and Patagonia's 'slow fashion' directly counters the throwaway model.

questions.q: Which innovation type generates the highest value to society according to the lecture?
options: Process Innovation
Product/Service Innovation
Business Model Innovation
Operational Innovation
Compliance Innovation
questions.explain: The lecture ranks three innovation types by value to business and society: Process Innovation (value to business), Product/Service Innovation (value to business + society), and Business Model Innovation (highest value to society). Business Model Innovation represents the deepest structural change and highest societal value because it fundamentally reframes how value is created and distributed.

questions.q: What is the key sustainability benefit of air-dyeing technology in textile manufacturing?
options: It reduces labor costs by 50 percent
It uses 25 liters less water per shirt compared to traditional dyeing
It eliminates the need for synthetic dyes
It increases production speed by 40 percent
It requires no specialized equipment or training
questions.explain: Air-dyeing technology is cited as a Process Innovation example. The lecture specifies that traditional fabric dyeing uses 25 liters of water per shirt, and air-dye technology eliminates this water consumption entirely. This is a concrete example of process innovation that reduces environmental impact while maintaining business value.

questions.q: Tranlin's production of paper and fertilizer from crop straws exemplifies which type of innovation?
options: Process Innovation only
Product/Service Innovation
Business Model Innovation
Regulatory Compliance Innovation
Supply Chain Innovation
questions.explain: Tranlin's product (paper and fertilizer from agricultural waste) is a Product/Service Innovation that creates value to both business and society. It is 100% compostable, restores soil, and sources materials from crop straws rather than forests. This provides both commercial viability and significant environmental benefit.

questions.q: What does 'Augmentation by Subtraction' mean in the context of product design innovation?
options: Reducing the price of a product without changing its features
Decreasing production volume to improve profit margins
Eliminating the product from the market entirely
Reducing corporate workforce to cut operational costs
Removing non-core features to solve the original problem more cleanly and efficiently
questions.explain: Augmentation by Subtraction is removing features to solve the core problem more cleanly. The lecture uses Southwest Airlines as the canonical example: by stripping down air travel to essentials, Southwest provides lower cost and better efficiency. Subtraction is classified as innovation because it challenges the assumption that innovation always means adding features.

questions.q: According to the lecture, why is Southwest Airlines considered an example of innovation through subtraction?
options: It removed safety features to reduce costs
It eliminated customer service to streamline operations
It stripped down the air travel offering to essentials, providing lower cost and higher value
It reduced the number of destinations served
It removed employee benefits to maximize shareholder returns
questions.explain: Southwest Airlines exemplifies Augmentation by Subtraction by stripping down air travel to essentials—no meals, no assigned seating, no frills—and delivering lower cost and competitive advantage. This demonstrates that removing features is a legitimate innovation strategy when those features do not solve the core problem (getting passengers to their destination affordably and reliably).

questions.q: What is the paradox of choice, and why does it matter for product design innovation?
options: Consumers always prefer more options regardless of cost
More options can reduce consumer satisfaction and waste design resources, contrary to traditional assumptions
Consumer choice leads to lower environmental impact
Paradox of choice only applies to luxury goods
More options always increase product value
questions.explain: The paradox of choice (referenced via Barry Schwartz's TED Talk) refers to the counterintuitive finding that more options can reduce consumer satisfaction and waste design resources. This supports the logic of Augmentation by Subtraction: by limiting features to the essential, a business can both improve customer experience and reduce resource waste.

questions.q: How does subtraction-based product design generate competitive advantage according to the lecture?
options: By lowering production costs through automation
By solving the original problem more cleanly while reducing resource waste and improving customer satisfaction
By eliminating competition through exclusive features
By increasing brand prestige through exclusivity
By forcing customers to upgrade more frequently
questions.explain: The lecture emphasizes that subtraction generates competitive advantage by solving the core problem more cleanly and efficiently. Southwest's example shows how removing non-essential services (meals, assigned seating) creates a simpler, lower-cost product that better serves customer needs (affordable, reliable transport). Subtraction also reduces waste, aligning with sustainability goals.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three augmentation modes discussed in the lecture?
options: Augmentation by Addition
Augmentation by Multiplication
Augmentation by Integration
Augmentation by Subtraction
All four are discussed
questions.explain: The lecture discusses three modes of augmentation: Addition (adding features), Multiplication (creating variants/configurations), and Subtraction (removing features). Augmentation by Integration is not mentioned. The three forms are presented to show different approaches to product evolution, with subtraction highlighted as often overlooked but valuable.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which augmentation mode is most likely to create the 'paradox of choice' problem?
options: Augmentation by Subtraction
Augmentation by Addition
Augmentation by Multiplication
Augmentation by Integration
All modes create equal choice paradox
questions.explain: Augmentation by Multiplication (multiplying product variants and configurations) generates complexity and the paradox of choice, which reduces consumer satisfaction. Too many options overwhelm customers and waste design resources. This is contrasted with Augmentation by Subtraction, which simplifies the offering to its core value proposition.

questions.q: What is the core distinction between eco-efficiency and sustainability vision as business strategies?
options: Eco-efficiency is faster to implement; Sustainability Vision is more ambitious
Eco-efficiency requires new technology; Sustainability Vision does not
Eco-efficiency costs more; Sustainability Vision is cheaper
Eco-efficiency benefits the environment; Sustainability Vision does not
Eco-efficiency optimizes current operations; Sustainability Vision reframes the company's purpose around solving societal challenges
questions.explain: Eco-efficiency (Internal/Present) optimizes existing operations to minimize waste and emissions. Sustainability Vision (External/Future) is more transformational—it reframes the company's fundamental purpose around addressing large societal challenges. The M&S 'Plan A' example shows this highest-level strategic commitment. One is incremental improvement; the other is strategic reorientation.

questions.q: Why might a company choose Resource Recovery as a circular business model instead of Circular Supplies?
options: Resource Recovery is less expensive to implement
Resource Recovery converts existing waste streams into valuable inputs, creating revenue from by-products or disposed products
Circular Supplies requires more technology investment
Resource Recovery has less environmental impact
Resource Recovery creates jobs more efficiently
questions.explain: Resource Recovery monetizes waste streams by recovering useful resources and energy from disposed products or by-products. The Adidas x Parley example shows how ocean plastic (a disposal problem) becomes a sellable product input. This differs from Circular Supplies, which substitutes virgin materials upfront. Both are circular, but Resource Recovery leverages existing 'waste' as a resource opportunity.

questions.q: Which sustainability debate position claims that consumption behavior, not supply-side technology, is the primary driver of environmental problems?
options: The extinction argument
The consumption argument
The technology argument
The regulatory argument
The growth argument
questions.explain: The lecture presents 'Sustainability challenges are largely a problem of consumption (消費)' as one of the three common debate positions. This locates responsibility with demand-side behavior—consumers choosing what and how much to buy—rather than supply-side factors like production methods or technology. This contrasts with the technology-focused position.

questions.q: How does the experience economy create both business value and sustainability value simultaneously?
options: By increasing consumer spending on durable goods
By selling intangible experiences that generate higher long-term satisfaction while producing less physical waste
By eliminating the need for product manufacturing
By shifting costs to consumers rather than businesses
By reducing the need for sustainable practices in production
questions.explain: The experience economy (commodity → good → service → experience) commands higher prices while generating less physical waste. Research cited in the lecture shows experiential purchases score 5.42 versus material purchases 4.67 at 4 weeks post-consumption (1–7 scale), indicating superior long-term satisfaction. This is a win-win: better margins and lower environmental footprint.

questions.q: What strategic question does the lecture pose about subtraction-based design in business competition?
options: How can a business eliminate competitors through subtraction?
How can a business compete and provide new value to customers by subtraction?
How can subtraction reduce the need for innovation?
How can subtraction eliminate regulatory compliance?
How can subtraction increase market share without environmental concern?
